Part VIII · AI-Era Product Management

Building AI-Powered Products

AI PRDs, evals, agents, cost, latency, trust and UX.

36 min read · 5 templates · 7 prompts

An AI-powered product doesn't behave the same way twice, costs money every time someone uses it, and has to earn the user's trust one answer at a time. Those three facts change how you specify it, measure it, price it and run it. This chapter shows the product manager what changes in each.

Why this matters

For thirty years, software products were deterministic. You wrote a requirement, engineering built it, QA checked that the same input produced the expected output, and you shipped. Marginal cost was close to zero, so pricing was mostly a question of value and competition. Trust came from reliability: once a feature worked, it kept working.

AI-powered products break all three assumptions.

  • Behavior is a distribution, not a specification. The same prompt can produce a great answer, a mediocre one and a confidently wrong one. You can’t specify the output; you can only specify how often it must be good, and what “good” means.
  • Cost scales with usage. Every answer has an inference cost. A feature that delights users can quietly destroy gross margin. Agentic features, which call models many times per task, make this worse.
  • Trust is earned per answer. Users can’t easily tell a right answer from a plausible wrong one. A single confident mistake in a high-stakes moment can cost more trust than a hundred good answers earn.

The result is that the PM’s job on an AI product expands. Quality becomes a product decision you specify with evals. Cost becomes a requirement with a gross-margin floor. Trust becomes a design problem with its own patterns. Autonomy becomes a dial you set per action, not a feature you ship. And regulation, for the first time in most enterprise PMs’ careers, becomes a product input rather than a legal review at the end.

This chapter covers each of those. Chapter 32 covers the other half of AI-era product management: using AI to do the PM job itself. Chapter 33 goes deeper on responsible AI and regulation.

Does this need AI at all?

The first question is the one teams skip. Google’s People + AI Research (PAIR) team makes it the opening chapter of the People + AI Guidebook: decide whether AI adds value before deciding how to build it.

AI is a good fit when the task involves judgment over messy inputs (language, images, logs, unstructured documents), when a probabilistic answer is useful even if it’s sometimes wrong, and when the cost of an error is low or can be caught. It’s a poor fit when the task has a correct, rule-based answer, when every error is expensive and hard to detect, or when users need to predict exactly what the system will do.

PAIR’s framing of precision versus recall is a practical tool here. Every AI feature makes two kinds of mistake: false positives (it says yes when the answer is no) and false negatives (it misses something real). They rarely cost the same. For Beacon, a false-positive root cause (“the deploy at 14:02 caused this”) can send an engineer to roll back the wrong service, which is expensive. A false negative (“I couldn’t determine the cause”) just means the engineer diagnoses it manually, which is the status quo. That asymmetry should shape the product: tune for precision, and make “I don’t know” a first-class answer.

Key ideaStart with the cost of being wrong

Before choosing a model or a pattern, write down what each kind of error costs the user and the business. That one table will drive your eval targets, your autonomy settings, your UX and, often, your pricing.

Workflows, agents and autonomy

Workflows versus agents

Anthropic’s widely cited essay “Building effective agents,” by Erik Schluntz and Barry Zhang, draws a distinction every AI PM needs. Workflows orchestrate models and tools through predefined code paths. Agents let the model direct its own process and tool use, in a loop, based on what it observes. Both are “agentic systems,” and they sit on a spectrum of patterns, from simple to complex:

Pattern What it does Use it when
Augmented model One model call with retrieval, tools or memory The task is a single step with the right context
Prompt chaining A fixed sequence of model calls, each feeding the next The task splits into predictable steps
Routing Classifies the input and sends it to a specialized path Different inputs need different handling
Parallelization Splits work into parallel calls, or runs the same call several times and votes Speed matters, or you want more confidence
Orchestrator-workers One model breaks the task down and delegates to others Subtasks can’t be predicted in advance
Evaluator-optimizer One model drafts, another critiques, in a loop Clear evaluation criteria exist and iteration helps
Autonomous agent The model uses tools in a loop until it reaches a goal or a stopping condition The task is open-ended and the steps can’t be predicted

The essay’s central advice is to start with the simplest pattern that works. Agentic systems trade latency and cost for capability. Many enterprise features work better as workflows, which are cheaper, faster and much easier to evaluate and audit. Use an agent only when the problem really is open-ended, and record the choice in the PRD as a decision with its rationale.

The same essay introduces the agent-computer interface: design the tools an agent uses as carefully as you’d design a human interface. Write tool descriptions the way you’d brief a junior developer, and design arguments so mistakes are hard to make. That’s product work, and in B2B platforms it often falls to the PM who owns the API.

Autonomy is a dial, set per action

Kevin Feng, David McDonald and Amy Zhang’s 2025 paper “Levels of Autonomy for AI Agents” gives product teams a useful vocabulary. It defines five levels by the user’s role, not the agent’s capability:

Level User’s role What the agent does
L1 Operator The user directs and decides; the agent carries out
L2 Collaborator The user and agent plan and execute together
L3 Consultant The agent leads and consults the user for expertise or preferences
L4 Approver The agent acts and involves the user only for risky or pre-specified situations
L5 Observer The agent acts fully autonomously; the user monitors

The paper’s key point is that autonomy is a design choice, separate from capability. A model that can act autonomously shouldn’t necessarily be allowed to.

For product specification, this book recommends setting autonomy per action class, not per product. An agent can sensibly be at L4 for reading logs and drafting a diagnosis, and at L2 for anything that writes to a production system. Pair that with a reversibility map: which actions can be undone cheaply, which are costly to reverse and which are irreversible. Irreversible actions need approval, dry-run modes or two-step confirmation, however good the model is.

Connectors, MCP and agent protocols

Agents are only as useful as what they can reach. In 2026 that increasingly runs through open protocols. The Model Context Protocol (MCP), which Anthropic introduced in late 2024, became the common way for AI applications to connect to tools and data. In December 2025 Anthropic donated MCP to the new Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation, co-founded with OpenAI and Block, and at that point Anthropic reported more than 10,000 active public MCP servers. Google’s Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol, hosted by the Linux Foundation since mid-2025, addresses a different problem: agents talking to other agents across organizations. The two are complementary, and the landscape is still moving.

For a B2B platform PM, the practical implication is that an MCP server is now a product surface, comparable to a public API. Customers’ agents (in Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot or their own harnesses) reach your product through it. It needs a scope, an authentication model, rate limits, versioning, documentation, and a pricing position. Treat it as a product, with an owner, rather than as an integration somebody builds on a Friday.

Evals: quality as a product decision

Why evals replace “it works”

In a deterministic product, QA checks whether a feature works. In an AI product, the question is how often it works, on which kinds of input, and how badly it fails when it doesn’t. The tool for answering that is an eval: a set of test cases, run automatically, each graded pass or fail, producing a quality score you can track over time and gate releases on.

Evals are where the PM’s definition of quality becomes executable. That’s why Lenny Rachitsky’s 2025 podcast with Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar billed evals as the hottest new skill for product builders, and why the PM (or a domain expert the PM designates) must own the eval’s definition of “good” rather than leaving it to engineering.

Start with error analysis

Hamel Husain and Shreya Shankar, whose evals course and FAQ are a widely used practitioner reference, put it bluntly: error analysis is “the most important activity in evals.” Their method:

  1. Read real traces. Pull about 30 real interactions (inputs, model outputs, tool calls). Read every one.
  2. Write free-form notes on what went wrong in each. Don’t use a rubric yet; rubrics written in advance narrow what you notice.
  3. Cluster the notes into a failure taxonomy: a named list of the ways the product fails.
  4. Keep going until you stop finding new failure types. That’s your signal that the taxonomy is complete enough for now.

The failure taxonomy becomes the eval’s structure and, often, the team’s backlog. Each recurring failure mode gets a fix, and if it persists, a dedicated test.

Husain and Shankar add several rules that are worth adopting as team policy:

  • Use binary pass/fail, not 1 to 5 scales. Rating scales produce inconsistent labels and drift toward the middle. If you need finer tracking, measure sub-components separately.
  • One narrow judge per failure mode. When you use a model to grade outputs (an “LLM-as-judge”), give it one specific failure to check. Validate each judge against human labels, and report how often it catches real failures and how often it correctly passes good outputs, separately, rather than a single “agreement” number.
  • Distrust generic metrics. “Helpfulness” scores and text-similarity metrics rarely track what users care about. Write evaluators for failures you’ve actually observed.
  • Name one accountable domain expert. Someone has to make the final call on what “good” means. On most product teams, that’s the PM or a domain expert the PM designates.

Capability, regression and consistency

Anthropic’s January 2026 guide “Demystifying evals for AI agents” adds vocabulary that’s useful for planning.

Capability evals measure what the product can’t yet do well. They should start with a low pass rate: they’re the hill you’re climbing. Regression evals protect what already works, and should pass at nearly 100% on every release. When a capability eval saturates, it graduates into the regression suite.

The guide also distinguishes two ways of counting success over several attempts, and for customer-facing products the difference is large:

  • pass@k is the probability that at least one of k attempts succeeds. It’s the right measure when a user can pick the best of several options.
  • pass^k is the probability that all k attempts succeed. It’s the right measure when a customer expects the product to work every time.

The arithmetic is unforgiving. A task that succeeds 75% of the time on any one try succeeds three times in a row only about 42% of the time (0.75 × 0.75 × 0.75). For an agent that runs the same kind of task hundreds of times a week, consistency, not best-case capability, is what customers experience.

Two more practical rules from the guide: start with 20 to 50 tasks drawn from real failures and user-reported bugs, balancing “should do” and “should not do” cases; and grade outcomes, not paths. For an agent, check whether the end state is right (the ticket was updated, the service is healthy), not whether it called tools in exactly the expected order, because agents often find valid routes nobody anticipated.

Are evals the new PRD?

A popular line in 2025 and 2026 holds that “evals are the new PRD.” Braintrust’s version of the argument is that static specs assume deterministic behavior, while evals define target behavior, acceptance criteria and regression thresholds in a form that can gate releases. Lisa Murkin, writing in Mind the Product, offers the counterpoint: golden datasets overfit, thirty examples are directional rather than proof, datasets drift away from real usage while looking healthy, and a dataset owned only by product recreates the old PRD’s problems.

This book’s position sits between them. Evals don’t replace the PRD; they become its acceptance criteria in executable form. The narrative PRD still carries the why, the who, the economics and the risk. The eval suite defines, precisely and testably, what “working” means.

The AI PRD

An AI PRD keeps everything a classic PRD has and adds a set of sections that classic PRDs never needed. Published AI PRD templates, such as Miqdad Jaffer and Paweł Huryn’s in The Product Compass and Product School’s, add model, data and prompt requirements, accuracy and hallucination limits, guardrails and drift monitoring. Jaffer and Huryn’s says little about inference cost or unit economics. Here’s the full set of differences.

Classic PRD What the AI PRD adds or changes
Deterministic functional requirements Behavior specified as eval sets with pass-rate targets per failure mode, plus consistency (pass^k) targets
Acceptance by QA test cases Acceptance by validated graders (code checks, calibrated model judges, human review) and regression thresholds in CI
A list of edge cases A failure taxonomy from error analysis, plus adversarial and “should refuse” cases
Performance and security requirements Adds latency budgets (time to first token, end to end), cost per task, model and fallback policy, and drift monitoring
Data model Data requirements: grounding sources, permissions, personal data handling, retention and feedback capture
UX flows Trust and failure UX: confidence, citations, correction, undo and escalation
Launch plan Staged autonomy: shadow mode, assisted, supervised, autonomous; kill switch
Pricing as a go-to-market item Unit economics as a requirement: a gross-margin floor per feature
Compliance review at the end Regulatory classification up front: risk tier, transparency duties, documentation obligations

The AI PRD addendum template at the end of this chapter covers every row.

Cost, latency and unit economics

The cost curve is falling, and your bill may still rise

The price of AI capability has fallen fast. Epoch AI’s 2025 analysis found that the price of reaching a fixed level of model performance fell by between 9x and 900x per year, depending on the task and threshold. GPT-4-level performance on one widely used knowledge benchmark went from about $37.50 per million tokens in March 2023 to about $0.18 by early 2025. Andreessen Horowitz’s Guido Appenzeller called the trend “LLMflation” and put it at roughly 10x per year at constant capability.

But a falling price per token doesn’t guarantee a falling cost per task. The steepest cuts apply to models that are no longer the frontier. Reasoning models think in long chains of tokens, and agents call models many times per task, so tokens per task tends to rise as products get more capable. Budget and price per task, not per token.

Gross margin is the number to watch

Classic SaaS businesses run gross margins of roughly 75 to 80% or more. AI products run much lower. ICONIQ’s 2026 State of AI report projects an average AI-product gross margin of about 53% for 2026, and Kyle Poyar’s 2026 monetization survey found a median target AI gross margin of about 50%, with only 12% of companies targeting 80% or more. If your margin slides toward those numbers, your finance team will notice before you do.

The levers a PM controls:

  • Model routing: send easy requests to small, cheap models and hard ones to frontier models. Often the single biggest lever.
  • Prompt caching: long, stable instructions and context can be cached so repeat calls cost a fraction of the original. Check your provider’s current pricing, because it changes often.
  • Workflow caching for agents: once an agent solves a recurring task, convert the successful path into deterministic code and call the model only when something unexpected happens. Andreessen Horowitz’s 2026 analysis of computer-use agents describes this as the pattern that makes agents economical on stable, high-volume work.
  • Budgets and stopping conditions: maximum steps, tokens, time and spend per task, with an escalation path when a limit is hit.
  • Latency design: stream output, keep time to first token low on interactive paths, use small models where speed matters, and run long agent tasks asynchronously.

Pricing AI

Seat-based pricing breaks when AI does the work that seats represented. If one agent replaces part of five people’s work, charging per seat charges less as you deliver more. That’s why AI pricing is in flux.

Model How it works Strength Risk
Seat Per user per month Simple, predictable Revenue falls as AI replaces human effort
Usage or credits Per token, call, action or credit Tracks cost Passes cost volatility to customers; bill anxiety
Outcome Per resolved ticket, resolved incident or qualified lead Aligns price with value Needs a measurable, attributable outcome; vendor carries performance risk
Hybrid Platform fee plus credits or outcomes Balances predictability and alignment More complex to explain and meter

The market is moving toward hybrids. Poyar’s 2026 survey of more than 230 B2B software and AI companies found hybrid pricing had become the most common model, at 37% of companies, and 29% using AI credits. The public examples show the experimentation. Intercom’s Fin AI agent has charged $0.99 per outcome. Salesforce launched Agentforce at $2 per conversation, then in May 2025 moved to Flex Credits priced at about $0.10 per action, and added per-user options later that year. And Cursor’s June 2025 move from request limits to included usage produced surprise charges and, in July, a public apology and refunds: a reminder that usage-linked pricing needs metering visibility and spend controls before it launches. Chapter 15 covers AI pricing in depth.

Trust and the UX of being wrong

Calibrated trust

The goal is calibrated trust: users trusting the system as much as its reliability warrants, and no more. PAIR’s guidebook builds its trust chapters around this idea, along with treating errors and graceful failure as part of the core flow rather than an edge case.

Microsoft’s Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction, published by Saleema Amershi and colleagues at CHI 2019 and validated with practitioners across twenty products, offer eighteen guidelines grouped into four moments. Paraphrased:

  • Initially: make clear what the system can do, and how well it can do it.
  • During interaction: time help to the context, show relevant information, and match social norms while mitigating bias.
  • When it’s wrong: make it easy to invoke, dismiss and correct; scope down when uncertain; and explain why it did what it did.
  • Over time: learn from behavior cautiously, invite granular feedback, provide global controls, and tell users when the system changes.

Use them as a launch-review checklist. Many AI trust failures map to one of them, often “make clear how well it can do it” or “scope services when in doubt.”

Patterns that work

  • Show sources and confidence wherever the user must act on an output. A root cause with three linked log lines is checkable; a bare assertion isn’t.
  • Make “I don’t know” a good answer. Design an explicit low-confidence state, and reward it in evals rather than penalizing it.
  • Make correction cheap with inline edits, regenerate and undo, and capture every correction as a label for evals.
  • Disclose AI. Users should know when they’re talking to an AI, especially in support. In the EU it’s increasingly a legal requirement, too.
  • Degrade gracefully to search, templates or a human when confidence is low or the model provider is down.
  • Design against rubber-stamping. “Human in the loop” fails silently when reviewers approve everything. Make wrong output easy to spot: highlight what changed, show the evidence, and sample approvals for audit.

What failure looks like in public

Four widely reported incidents illustrate the failure modes PMs must design against:

  • Air Canada (2024). A support chatbot told a customer they could claim a bereavement fare retroactively. A Canadian tribunal held the airline responsible for what its chatbot said, rejecting the argument that the bot was a separate entity. Lesson: you own your AI’s statements. Ground policy answers in approved sources and show them.
  • Cursor (2025). An AI support agent invented a login policy that didn’t exist, and users cancelled before a co-founder corrected it publicly. Lesson: disclose AI agents, and restrict policy statements to retrieved, approved content.
  • Replit (2025). During a code freeze, an AI coding agent ran destructive commands against a user’s live database, then misreported whether recovery was possible. Replit separated development and production databases afterward. Lesson: least privilege, environment separation and approval for irreversible actions.
  • Deloitte Australia (2025). A government report produced with AI assistance contained fabricated citations and a fabricated quote; the firm issued a corrected report and refunded part of the fee. Lesson: any AI-assisted deliverable needs citation verification and disclosure.

Data, flywheels and moats

Every AI strategy deck has a data flywheel: more usage produces more data, which makes the product better, which attracts more usage. Many teams assume a flywheel they don’t actually have. Usage compounds only when it produces labels (signals of what was good or bad), those labels feed evals or model improvements, and users can see the improvement.

In B2B, there’s a further constraint: enterprise contracts often forbid training on customer data. The flywheel may have to run on per-customer context (runbooks, history, preferences), on your own eval sets, and on aggregate signals customers have consented to share. Write feedback capture into the requirements: what signal, under which consent and contract terms, stored where.

Model access isn’t a moat; every competitor can call the same models. The defensible advantages in 2026 are workflow integration and switching costs, proprietary context (the customer-specific knowledge your product accumulates), distribution, and trust. Chapter 16 covers defensibility in depth.

Regulation: a product input now

Regulation used to arrive at the end of an enterprise product cycle, as a legal review. For AI products it needs to arrive at the start, because the evidence regulators require (risk management, logging, human oversight, accuracy testing, documentation) has to be built into the product, not bolted on.

A snapshot as of late 2026, which Chapter 33 covers in depth. This is not legal advice, and dates should be confirmed with counsel before you rely on them.

  • EU AI Act. The Act entered into force in August 2024. Prohibited practices and AI-literacy duties applied from February 2025, and obligations for general-purpose AI models from August 2025. Transparency obligations, such as telling people they’re interacting with AI, apply from August 2026. In July 2026 the EU adopted the “Digital Omnibus” amendment (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744), which postponed the high-risk obligations: stand-alone high-risk systems now from December 2027, and AI embedded in regulated products from August 2028.
  • NIST AI Risk Management Framework. A voluntary US framework built on four functions (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage), with a 2024 Generative AI Profile listing risks specific to generative AI, such as confabulation. Widely used in enterprise risk programs.
  • ISO/IEC 42001. The first certifiable AI management system standard, published in late 2023. It’s becoming the AI counterpart of ISO 27001 in enterprise security questionnaires.

For a PM, the practical step is to record in the PRD whether you’re a provider or a deployer of each AI system, its likely risk tier, and the transparency and documentation duties that follow. Even where obligations are years away, enterprise customers will ask for this documentation in security reviews now.

How to apply it

Here’s the lifecycle for building an AI-powered feature or product, from idea to scale.

  1. Write the cost-of-error table. For each kind of mistake (false positive, false negative, harmful output, wrong action), write what it costs the user and the business.
  2. Decide whether AI is the right tool. If a rule-based solution meets the need, use it. If not, state why AI adds value.
  3. Choose the simplest pattern. Start at the top of the workflow-to-agent table and move down only when a simpler pattern fails. Record the decision.
  4. Set autonomy per action class. Build the reversibility map. Default anything that changes a system of record to L2 (human approval) until evidence supports more.
  5. Prototype and run error analysis. Put a prototype in front of real or realistic inputs, read at least 30 traces, and build the failure taxonomy.
  6. Build the eval suite. Turn the taxonomy into 20 to 50 tasks with binary graders. Separate capability from regression evals. Validate any model judges against human labels. Set pass-rate and pass^k targets with your domain expert.
  7. Build the cost model. Estimate tokens and model calls per task, cost per task at expected volume, and gross margin at the proposed price. Set a margin floor. Identify routing and caching levers.
  8. Design the trust UX. Sources, confidence, “I don’t know,” correction, undo, escalation, disclosure. Review against the human-AI interaction guidelines.
  9. Classify the regulatory exposure. Provider or deployer, risk tier, transparency duties, documentation. Bring counsel in now.
  10. Roll out in stages. Shadow mode (the AI runs, users don’t see it, you compare to humans); assisted (users see suggestions); supervised (the AI acts with approval); autonomous for allowlisted actions. Move between stages on eval and production evidence, not on the calendar.
  11. Monitor in production. Track quality on sampled production traffic, cost per task, latency, user corrections and escalations. Re-run regression evals on every model, prompt or provider change.
  12. Close the loop. Every production failure becomes a new eval case. Review the failure taxonomy monthly.
For product leaders

Make the eval suite, the cost model and the model register required artifacts in your portfolio’s Product 360 for every AI-powered product, and review them in the monthly product review alongside the dashboard. AI products that aren’t measured this way drift in quality and margin without anyone noticing, until a customer or the CFO does.

The AI lens: using AI to build AI products

There’s a recursion worth exploiting here: AI is very good at helping you build the artifacts this chapter describes, as long as you keep the judgment human.

  • Drafting eval cases. A model can generate dozens of candidate test inputs per failure mode, including adversarial and “should refuse” cases you didn’t think of. You and your domain expert curate them.
  • Clustering error notes. After you’ve written free-form notes on traces, a model can propose a first failure taxonomy. Check it against your notes; the model will merge categories that matter.
  • Writing judge prompts. A model can draft a narrow judge for one failure mode. You must still validate it against human labels. An unvalidated judge is a second model’s opinion, not a measurement.
  • Building the cost model. Give a harness your expected volumes, token estimates and provider prices and it can produce a scenario model in minutes. Check every input yourself.
  • Red-teaming. A model can play an adversarial user, a prompt injection in a retrieved document, or a confused customer. It finds different weaknesses than your team does.

The guardrail: never let a model grade its own work unvalidated, and never let it decide what “good” means. Those are the two decisions that make an eval meaningful.

The Beacon case: the wrong rollback

Beacon caseWhat happened

Three weeks into the Beacon Agents design-partner pilot, a responder at a retail customer accepts the agent’s diagnosis that a deploy to the checkout service caused a latency spike, and rolls it back. The real cause was a database failover in a different region. The rollback takes checkout down for eleven minutes during a sale. The customer’s VP of IT Operations calls Northlight’s CEO.

The immediate response. You pause the pilot’s ability to propose rollbacks, keeping diagnosis on. You write to the customer within 24 hours explaining what happened, what you’ve changed and what you’ll do next. The incident goes in the decision log and the risk register, and it becomes the first entry in a new AI incident review process (Chapter 33).

Error analysis. You and the applied AI engineers pull 120 pilot traces and read them. Free-form notes cluster into a failure taxonomy of seven modes. The top three:

  1. Recency bias. The agent over-weights the most recent deploy, even when timing doesn’t fit.
  2. Single-region blindness. The agent doesn’t check infrastructure events outside the affected service’s region.
  3. Overconfident framing. Diagnoses are worded with the same certainty whether the evidence is strong or thin.

None of these was in the original PRD, which defined quality as “accurate root cause.”

The eval suite. You turn the taxonomy into 48 tasks built from real incidents, half “should diagnose” and half “should say I’m not sure.” Each has a binary grader: a code check for whether cited evidence exists and matches the timeline, and a narrow model judge for overconfident framing, validated against 150 labels from two SREs. Recency bias and region blindness become capability evals; the existing behaviors that worked become a regression suite.

The targets. With Priya’s team as domain experts, you set the bar: diagnosis accepted by responders in at least 60% of incidents; an “I’m not sure” rate between 15% and 30% (lower means overconfidence, higher means low value); zero rollback proposals where the cited evidence doesn’t match the timeline. Because responders see the agent in every incident, you track pass^3 on the regression suite, not just single-run accuracy.

Autonomy and UX. Rollback proposals move from L3 to L2: the agent can propose, but the UI shows the timeline evidence side by side with the change, and the approver must confirm the specific service and region. Every diagnosis now displays its evidence and an explicit confidence band.

Cost. The fix isn’t free. Checking cross-region infrastructure events adds three tool calls and about 40% more tokens per diagnosis. Your cost model shows Beacon Agents’ gross margin falling from 72% toward 66% at current pricing. You route the first-pass triage to a smaller model and cache the stable runbook context, which brings the projected margin back to about 71%. The margin floor goes in the AI PRD: 70%.

Pricing. The incident sharpens the per-resolved-incident pricing question. Marcus, the economic buyer, likes paying for outcomes, but his CFO asks who pays when the agent makes an incident worse. You add an outcome definition (incident resolved, with Beacon’s diagnosis accepted, and no reopening within 24 hours) and a credit policy for agent-caused incidents to the pricing proposal for Chapter 15.

The result. Six weeks later the pilot restarts with the new evals gating every release. Diagnosis acceptance reaches 64%, the “I’m not sure” rate settles at 22%, and there have been no mismatched rollback proposals. The retail customer stays in the pilot and, at Northlight Live, agrees to be a reference customer for diagnosis, though not yet for autonomous action.

Prompts

✦ PromptOpen-code a batch of AI traces
Goal: Get a fast first pass of error notes on real traces, to speed up (not replace) your own error analysis.
Paste in: 20 to 40 traces (input, output, tool calls, final outcome), with customer data removed or using an approved tool, plus a one-paragraph description of what the feature is supposed to do.

For each trace below, write one or two sentences of free-form notes on anything that went wrong or looks risky: wrong facts, unsupported claims, missed context, bad tool use, overconfident tone, unsafe action, poor format. If nothing went wrong, write "OK." Don't score with a rating scale. Don't group the notes yet.

Then, separately, propose a draft failure taxonomy: 5 to 10 named failure modes, each with a one-line definition and the trace numbers that show it.

[feature description]
[traces]

Check the output: read at least 15 traces yourself before you look at the model's notes, then compare. Expect the model to miss domain-specific failures and to merge modes you'd keep separate. The final taxonomy is yours.
✦ PromptGenerate eval cases for one failure mode
Goal: Build a balanced set of test cases quickly.
Paste in: the failure mode's name and definition, three real example traces that show it, and three that show correct behavior.

Generate 30 eval cases for this failure mode in [feature]: [name and definition].
- 15 cases where a correct system should succeed or act, and 15 where it should refuse, ask for more information, or say it isn't sure.
- Vary difficulty: include obvious cases and subtle ones.
- Include at least 5 adversarial cases (misleading context, conflicting evidence, an instruction hidden inside retrieved content).
- For each case give: the input, the context the system would have, the expected outcome (not the exact wording), and a one-line pass/fail criterion.

Base the cases on the real examples; don't invent product capabilities the examples don't show.

[examples]

Check the output: have your domain expert review every case. Delete any whose expected outcome you'd argue about; ambiguous cases poison an eval.
✦ PromptDraft and validate a model judge
Goal: Create a narrow LLM-as-judge for one failure mode, plus a plan to validate it.
Paste in: the failure mode's definition, 10 labeled examples (5 pass, 5 fail) with the reason for each label.

Write a judge prompt that checks one thing only: [failure mode]. The judge must return PASS or FAIL and a one-sentence reason quoting the part of the output that drove the decision. Include the definition, the labeled examples as few-shot guidance, and instructions to ignore every other quality dimension.

Then write a validation plan: how many human labels I need, how to split them into development and test sets, how to calculate the true positive rate and true negative rate, and what rates I should require before trusting the judge to gate releases.

[definition and examples]

Check the output: run the judge on a held-out set you labeled yourself. Don't use it to gate releases until you've measured both rates on data it hasn't seen.
✦ PromptBuild a first AI cost model
Goal: See the gross-margin effect of an AI feature before it ships.
Paste in: the steps the feature performs, the model for each step, estimated input and output tokens per call, calls per task, current provider prices (with the date), expected monthly task volume and the planned price.

Build a cost model for [feature] with:
1. A per-task cost table by step, including caching assumptions.
2. Monthly cost, revenue and gross margin at low, expected and high volume.
3. The cost per task at which gross margin falls below [floor]%.
4. Three levers to reduce cost (routing, caching, converting recurring paths to deterministic code, budgets), each with an estimated saving and the quality risk it introduces.
5. Sensitivity to tokens per task rising 50% and prices rising 20%.

Show your formulas. Don't invent prices; use only the ones I gave you, and flag any input you had to assume.

[inputs]

Check the output: recompute one scenario by hand. Confirm prices against the provider's current pricing page before sharing the model with finance.
✦ PromptReview an agent's autonomy design
Goal: Find autonomy and permission gaps before a customer does.
Paste in: the agent's list of actions and tools, the permissions each tool has, the proposed autonomy level per action, and the approval UX.

Review this agent design for [product] as a skeptical security reviewer and SRE.
1. For each action, classify reversibility (cheap, costly, irreversible) and say whether the proposed autonomy level (L1 operator to L5 observer) is appropriate. Recommend changes.
2. Identify any tool with broader permissions than its actions need.
3. List ways a prompt injection in retrieved content or tool output could cause a harmful action, and the control that would stop each.
4. Check stopping conditions and budgets. What happens when a limit is hit?
5. Assess whether the approval UX would let a tired reviewer rubber-stamp a wrong action, and suggest design changes.
Finish with the five changes you'd require before production.

[design]

Check the output: walk through the riskiest action end to end with your engineering lead and confirm the model's reading of the permissions is correct.
✦ PromptRed-team an AI feature
Goal: Find failure modes your team hasn't imagined.
Paste in: the feature description, the system instructions or a summary of them, the user types, and the tools and data it can access.

Act as a red team for [feature]. Generate 25 test scenarios across these categories: confused or mistaken users, adversarial users, prompt injection through documents or tool outputs, requests outside the intended scope, high-stakes situations where a wrong answer causes harm, attempts to extract other customers' data, and situations where the right answer is "I don't know." For each, give the scenario, what a safe response looks like and what failure would look like.

Rank the five scenarios you think are most likely to cause real harm in production, and explain why.

[feature details]

Check the output: run the top-ranked scenarios against the real system. Add every failure you find to the eval suite.
✦ PromptReview an AI PRD for gaps
Goal: Make sure an AI PRD covers what classic PRDs miss.
Paste in: the PRD and its AI addendum.

Review this PRD for an AI-powered feature. For each of these areas, say whether it's covered well, covered weakly or missing, and quote the relevant text: cost of error; choice of pattern and autonomy; failure taxonomy and eval targets; consistency targets; model, fallback and data requirements; cost per task and margin floor; latency budget; trust and failure UX; regulatory classification; staged rollout and kill switch. Then list the three gaps most likely to cause a production incident or a margin problem, and the question I should ask the team about each.

[PRD]

Check the output: confirm each "covered well" against the PRD yourself. Bring the three questions to your next review.

Anti-patterns

Anti-patternVibe checks

The team tries a dozen prompts, the answers look good, and the feature ships. Quality is never measured, so nobody notices when a model update makes it worse. If there’s no eval suite gating releases, there’s no quality bar.

Anti-patternAgents for everything

A multi-step agent is built for a task a single model call with the right context could do. It’s slower, costlier and harder to evaluate. Start with the simplest pattern that works.

Anti-patternOne autonomy level for the whole product

The agent is either fully supervised (and users find it tedious) or fully autonomous (and someone gets hurt). Set autonomy per action class, based on reversibility.

Anti-patternThe margin surprise

The feature succeeds, usage grows, and finance discovers gross margin has fallen ten points. Cost per task and a margin floor belong in the PRD, and on the monthly dashboard.

Anti-patternUnvalidated judges

A model grades the outputs, the scores look great, and nobody has checked whether the judge agrees with humans. An unvalidated judge measures nothing.

Anti-patternHuman in the loop, in name only

Every action requires approval, reviewers approve 99.8% of them in under two seconds, and the one wrong action sails through. Design approval screens that make wrong output easy to see, and audit a sample of approvals.

Anti-patternRegulation at the end

The product is built, and then legal asks for logging, documentation and human-oversight evidence it doesn’t have. Classify regulatory exposure at the start, and build the evidence in.

Checklist

Key takeaways

  • AI products behave like distributions, cost money per use and earn trust one answer at a time. Specifying, measuring, pricing and running them works differently than it does for classic software.
  • Start with the cost of being wrong. It sets your eval targets, autonomy levels and UX, and often your pricing.
  • Use the simplest pattern that works. Reserve agents for open-ended tasks, and set autonomy per action class based on how reversible each action is.
  • Evals are the PRD’s acceptance criteria in executable form. Build them from error analysis on real traces, use binary graders and validated judges, and track consistency, not just best-case accuracy.
  • Cost per task and gross margin are product requirements. Falling token prices don’t guarantee falling task costs, and AI margins run well below classic SaaS.
  • Design for calibrated trust: show evidence, make “I don’t know” a good answer, make correction cheap and stop human review from becoming a rubber stamp.
  • Regulation is now a product input. Record your role, risk tier and obligations at the start, and build the evidence into the product.
32
Part VIII · AI-Era Product Management

The AI-Augmented Product Manager

AI workflows across every PM task, with the guardrails.

46 min read · 6 templates · 10 prompts

Most product managers now use AI at work, and most of them use it to produce documents faster. This chapter shows how to use it on the thinking as well: pointing the harness at discovery and decisions as well as documents, giving it the context it needs, checking what it produces, and keeping the judgment, the relationships and the final call with you.

Why this matters

The first wave of AI adoption among PMs went to production work. In Noam Segal and Lenny Rachitsky’s December 2025 survey of 1,750 tech workers, the most common primary uses among PMs were writing PRDs (21.5%), building mockups and prototypes (19.8%) and improving communication such as email and presentations (18.5%). User research sat at 4.7% and roadmap ideas at 1.1%. Those are self-reported shares, but the shape is clear: AI is helping PMs produce artifacts, and it has barely touched the upstream work that decides which artifacts are worth producing.

PMs also said they wanted that to change. User research showed the largest gap between current and desired use of any task in the survey, about 27 points, and mockups and prototypes were the most wanted future use. What’s missing is a way of working that gets AI into discovery and decision-making without degrading either.

The benefits people report are real enough to take seriously. In the same survey, 63% of PMs said AI saves them four or more hours a week, and over 70% reported better work quality. Across all roles, though, 92.4% of respondents also reported at least one significant downside, so plan for the gains and the failures together.

Marty Cagan points to a larger problem. In his July 2026 essay “The AI Productivity Paradox,” he argues that teams are using AI to ship faster while their outcomes stay flat, because most of them apply it to a project model that he describes as “designed to deliver output, rather than outcomes.” Atlassian’s State of Teams 2026 report, a vendor survey of 12,035 knowledge workers and 173 Fortune 1000 executives, puts numbers on the pattern: 89% of the executives said AI increases speed of work, while only 6% were sure they had clear examples of organization-wide AI ROI. The same report found that 85% of knowledge workers use AI at work but only 29% have embedded it in their workflows.

That last gap is the practical one for you. Using AI means opening a chat when you remember to. Embedding it means a defined set of recurring tasks where the harness has the right context, the right access and a known check, so the work gets done the same way every week and gets better over time.

Be careful, too, with how fast AI makes you feel. In METR’s July 2025 randomized trial, 16 experienced open-source developers worked 246 real issues with and without AI tools. With AI allowed, they took 19% longer, yet afterwards they believed they had been about 20% faster. METR’s authors stress that this was a snapshot of early-2025 tools in one setting, and in February 2026 they published newer data on late-2025 tools, noting that the early-2025 results are out of date. The lesson for a PM doesn’t depend on the exact number: measure what AI does to your outcomes and cycle times.

This chapter gives you a working system for the AI-augmented PM role:

  1. A workflow map that shows where AI helps across your job, how much to trust it at each step and what stays human.
  2. A harness setup: projects, connectors, skills and scheduled tasks, arranged on an automation ladder you climb one rung at a time.
  3. A context pack that turns your Product 360 into the context every AI task starts from.
  4. A prompt library that the whole team shares, tests and improves.
  5. A verification standard and a usage policy that keep the work accurate and confidential.
  6. A weekly operating routine that makes all of it a habit.

Core concepts and frameworks

Build to learn before build to earn

Cagan’s answer to the paradox is a sequence. Strong teams use AI first to build to learn: generating and testing many candidate solutions with customers and stakeholders, quickly and cheaply, to establish value and viability. Only then do they use it to build to earn: producing the reliable, scalable, commercial-quality version. In an October 2026 follow-up, he argues that because AI has cut the cost of building, the hard part has moved to working out what to build, which puts experimentation and discovery at the center of the job.

For an enterprise PM, the practical consequence is where you spend your AI time. If most of it goes to drafting PRDs and status updates faster, you’re accelerating the part of the job that matters least. Cagan goes further in a February 2026 essay on product coaching: using AI only to aggregate requests, generate roadmaps and write PRDs exposes that work as theater, because an engineer or an agent could do it.

Shift the budget upstream. B2B PMs sit on more unread evidence than almost anyone in the company: call recordings, support tickets, win/loss notes, CRM histories, partner feedback and usage data that nobody has read end to end. A harness with connectors changes what one person can know. Chapter 01 covers discovery synthesis in depth; this chapter shows how to make it routine.

Prototyping is the other half of build to learn. Colin Matthews sorts AI prototyping tools into three classes: chatbots with a canvas for single-page mockups, cloud development environments for multi-page prototypes you can share, and developer assistants that work in a real codebase. His advice is to add one feature at a time with specific requests and to put the prototype in front of users before engineering builds anything. Chapter 04 covers the fidelity ladder and usability testing; in your workflow map, prototyping sits on the learning side, judged by what customers did with it.

Key ideaPoint AI at the decision, then at the document

For each piece of work, ask what decision it supports. Use AI first to gather and test the evidence behind the decision, then to write the document that records it. Drafting speed doesn’t help when the decision behind the document is wrong.

The jagged frontier

The best evidence on where AI helps knowledge workers comes from a 2023 field experiment by Fabrizio Dell’Acqua, Ethan Mollick and colleagues from Harvard Business School and other institutions, run with 758 BCG consultants. On 18 realistic consulting tasks inside the model’s capability, consultants using GPT-4 completed 12.2% more tasks, finished 25.1% faster and produced work rated about 40% higher in quality. On one task designed to sit just outside the model’s capability, consultants without AI got the right answer 84% of the time; with AI, 60 to 70%.

Mollick calls this the jagged frontier. AI is strong at some tasks and weak at others that look equally hard to a person, and you only find the line by using it. Worse, the failure outside the frontier is hard to see, because the output looks just as fluent when it’s wrong. Mollick warns that the danger is people who stop paying attention once the model seems competent.

Mollick also describes two working styles: centaurs hand whole tasks to AI and keep others, while cyborgs interleave with the model at a fine grain. Both can work if you know which tasks sit where.

For PM work, a useful map looks like this:

PM task Typical frontier position Why
Summarizing a call, reformatting a document, drafting a follow-up Inside Source material is supplied and the output is easy to check
Clustering interview themes, mining tickets, first-pass win/loss Inside, with traceability Strong at grouping, weak at rare signals; every theme must link to sources
Drafting a PRD or narrative from your brief Inside Your thinking supplies the substance; the model supplies structure and prose
Mapping edge, error, empty and permission states Inside Systematic enumeration is a strength
Explaining a metric movement Edge Good at hypotheses, prone to confident causal stories the data can’t support
Competitive claims and market numbers Edge Needs dated sources; models confabulate specifics
Statements about a named customer or account Outside unless sourced Errors here damage relationships and trust
Prioritization, trade-offs, strategy calls Outside as decider, inside as critic Use it to red-team your call, never to make it

The rule that follows: set the depth of verification by frontier position, task by task. Chapter 31 applies the same logic to the AI features you build; here you apply it to yourself.

The harness and its parts

A harness is the AI environment you work in: a chat application, a desktop agent, a coding tool or an assistant built into your company’s tools. In 2026 the mainstream harnesses share a common set of parts, and a PM should understand each as a capability, whatever the brand.

  • Projects (sometimes called workspaces, custom assistants or Gems): a persistent space with its own instructions, its own knowledge files and its own history. Anthropic’s Claude, for example, gives each project a knowledge base and project instructions, and on team plans lets you share a project with colleagues as view-only or editable. This is where your product’s context pack lives.
  • Connectors: live, permissioned access to the systems where your evidence sits, such as the backlog, CRM, call recordings, support tickets, product analytics, documents and chat. Most are now built on the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard for connecting AI applications to external data, tools and workflows, supported across Claude, ChatGPT, VS Code, Cursor and others. Chapter 19 covers connectors for analysis in detail. Every connector is also an access grant, which matters for the usage policy below.
  • Skills: packaged procedures. Anthropic introduced Agent Skills in October 2025 as folders of instructions, scripts and resources that the model loads only when a task calls for them, and in December 2025 published them as an open standard so they work across platforms. A skill turns “the way we write release notes” or “the way we review a PRD” into something every PM’s harness does the same way.
  • Agents and scheduled tasks: knowledge-work agents that carry out multi-step work across files and connected tools, then return it for review. Several harnesses can now run a saved task daily, weekly or monthly without you starting it, with approval prompts before significant actions.

Anthropic’s guidance for its own coding agent draws a distinction that matters for everything above. A prompt, a memory file or a skill is read by the model, which usually follows it but not always. A permission setting, a blocked action or an admin control is enforced by the harness every time. Put anything that must always or never happen in the second layer. “Never send email without my approval” belongs in a permission, not in a polite instruction.

The automation ladder

Erik Schluntz and Barry Zhang, in Anthropic’s “Building effective agents,” separate workflows, where models and tools follow predefined steps, from agents, where the model directs its own process. Their advice is to start with the simplest thing that works, because agents trade cost and latency for flexibility, and many needs are met by one well-built call with good context and examples. Their patterns include prompt chaining (one step’s output feeds the next), routing, parallelization, orchestrator and workers, and evaluator-optimizer, where one pass drafts and a second pass critiques against criteria.

Most PM automation should be a workflow. A weekly metrics digest is prompt chaining. A PRD review is evaluator-optimizer. Open-ended agents with write access come last, if at all.

This book arranges the path as an automation ladder with six rungs. It’s a Product 360 synthesis, not a published framework:

Climb a rung only when the work on the rung below is stable: the prompt gives consistently good output, the checks catch the known failures and someone owns it. A prompt that only works when you babysit it isn’t ready to become a scheduled task. A scheduled task whose output you no longer read has quietly become rung 6 without the gate.

Microsoft’s 2025 Work Trend Index, a vendor survey of 31,000 knowledge workers across 31 markets, calls a person who builds, delegates to and manages agents an agent boss. Once you run scheduled tasks, that’s you: set the brief, check the work and own the result, as you would for a junior teammate.

Context engineering: the Product 360 as context

In June 2025, Shopify’s CEO Tobi Lütke said he preferred the term context engineering to prompt engineering, describing it as providing all the context a task needs to be plausibly solvable; Andrej Karpathy endorsed the term. Simon Willison predicted it would stick because its obvious meaning matches its intended one. Anthropic’s Applied AI team then laid out the method: context engineering curates everything the model sees (instructions, tools, data and history), and the goal is to “find the smallest set of high-signal tokens” that produces the result you want.

Four of their findings translate directly to PM work:

  • Context rot. As the context window fills, recall degrades. More material is not better. Pasting forty documents into a chat can produce worse answers than pasting the four that matter.
  • The right altitude. Instructions should sit between brittle step-by-step rules and vague guidance. Start minimal, then add instructions and examples in response to failures you actually observe.
  • Examples over rules. A few diverse, canonical examples (a great PRD, a great exec update) beat long lists of edge-case rules.
  • Just-in-time retrieval. Keep lightweight references to where things live and load them when needed. A short always-loaded brief plus referenced documents usually works best.

Your Product 360 (Chapter 00) is already the smallest set of high-signal context about your product: personas, vision, strategy, metrics tree, pricing, competitive map, decision log. A PM who has built a Product 360 has done most of the context engineering already. The context pack packages it for the harness: a one-to-two-page brief that every task loads, plus pointers to the full artifacts that load on demand. A PM without a Product 360 gets generic answers, because the model fills the gaps with averages from everybody else’s products.

NoteWhy generic answers happen

When a model lacks your context, it doesn’t say “I don’t know your buyer.” It writes for a plausible average buyer. The output reads well and fits nobody. If the answers you get could apply to any B2B product, the fix is almost always context, not a cleverer prompt.

The prompt library and skills

A prompt library is the team’s shared, versioned set of prompts for recurring work, each with an owner, the inputs it needs, the context to attach, what good looks like and how to check it. Anthropic’s prompt-engineering guidance sets the order of work: define success criteria first, have a way to test against them, then write the prompt. An entry without a “what good looks like” line and two or three test inputs can’t be tested, so nobody can tell when it stops working.

Treat the library as a product with an owner (usually product ops, Chapter 28), a review date on every entry and a promotion rule: when two or more PMs use a prompt every week, turn it into a skill so the procedure and its checks travel together. Skills also keep the always-loaded context short, because the model reads a skill’s full procedure only when it needs it.

Verification: give the work a check to run

NIST’s Generative AI Profile (AI 600-1, July 2024) lists twelve risks of generative AI. Two of them describe a PM’s daily exposure. Confabulation is confidently stated but false content, including outputs that diverge from the input; NIST calls it a natural result of how these models work. Human-AI configuration covers automation bias and over-reliance: the human stops checking.

The defense is a check you can run, phrased as pass or fail. Anthropic’s guidance for its coding agent makes the point that without a check, the model can only judge whether work looks finished, and you end up as the test suite. For PM work, the standard checks are:

  • Every number traces to a named source and date.
  • Every customer quote carries a source ID (call, ticket or interview) and appears verbatim in that source.
  • Every competitor claim has a dated source.
  • No commitment, date or scope appears that you didn’t make.
  • Every named customer, account or person is spelled correctly and described accurately.
  • The output answers the brief; nothing in the brief is missing.

Two refinements make reviews work. First, review against the brief, not in general: a reviewer told to find problems will always find something, so tell it what to check and what to skip (style, usually). Second, use a fresh session for the review, so the reviewer isn’t anchored on the draft’s reasoning. This is evaluator-optimizer applied to your own documents, and it’s the same eval discipline Chapter 31 asks you to apply to your product.

Confidentiality and approved tools

The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025 edition) was written for teams building AI applications, but three of its risks apply directly to a PM’s own harness:

  • Prompt injection. A customer email, web page or document read through a connector can contain instructions the model follows. An agent summarizing inbound mail can be told, by the mail, to do something else.
  • Sensitive information disclosure. Customer data, unannounced financials or personal data pasted into a tool your company hasn’t approved, or a consumer account that may retain it.
  • Excessive agency. An agent with permission to send, write or delete acting without review.

The controls are boring and effective: use only company-approved tools and enterprise accounts; classify data and know which classes may go where; give connectors the narrowest scope that works (read-only wherever possible); require a human approval before any send, write or external action; and treat anything an agent reads from outside the company as data, never as instructions.

Regulation now touches this too. Article 4 of the EU AI Act, applicable since 2 February 2025, requires providers and deployers of AI systems to take measures so that staff who use AI on their behalf have sufficient AI literacy, considering their knowledge, the context and the people affected. Amendments have been proposed, so confirm the current wording with your legal team before you rely on it. A written team usage policy plus a short onboarding is a practical part of meeting it. Chapter 33 covers AI regulation in full.

What not to delegate

Talks from the Lenny and Friends Summit, published in September 2026, return often to judgment. Robby Stein of Google Search argued that as building gets easier, a PM’s value centers on judgment and taste; Tamar Yehoshua of Atlassian argued that PM, engineering and design aren’t collapsing into one role, but each can now do far more; Stripe’s Katie Dill urged teams to use AI to “raise the ceiling, not just the floor.” Ami Vora of Anthropic and Yehoshua both said there is no single right AI workflow yet. Norms are still forming, which is why your team should write its own.

Keep these with you, every time:

  • Decisions and trade-offs. AI can lay out options and attack your reasoning. You decide, and you can explain why without the transcript.
  • Commitments. Dates, scope and promises to customers, partners or executives.
  • Prioritization calls. The model can score; it can’t own the consequences.
  • Relationship moments. Escalations, bad news, negotiations, coaching and anything where the other person needs to know you were there.
  • Final say on what ships, and on anything that carries your name. If you haven’t read it, don’t sign it.

Cagan’s coaching essay offers a middle ground: configure a model with your company’s strategic context and use it as a coach that critiques your thinking and names your mistakes. Leaders, he adds, still need a human coach, because leadership problems are about people, politics and power.

Team adoption: leadership, lab and crowd

Individual skill doesn’t make a team AI-augmented. Ethan Mollick’s model for organizational adoption has three parts. Leadership sets the urgency and paints a concrete picture of AI-enabled work. The Lab, a small group, builds and tests tools, benchmarks and demos. The Crowd, everyone else, learns by using AI and shares what works. Mollick also warns about secret cyborgs: people who use AI but hide it, out of fear of punishment, lost respect or a bigger workload. Hidden use means hidden mistakes and unshared gains.

In a product organization, the mapping is natural. Leadership is the VP of Product modeling AI use openly in reviews. The Lab is product ops plus one or two curious PMs who own the library, the skills and the context packs. The Crowd is every PM, contributing prompts and reporting failures. The norm to state out loud: AI use is expected and disclosed, never hidden, and finding a better workflow earns credit, not more work.

For product leaders

Measure adoption by outcomes and embedded routines, not by seat licenses or self-reported hours. Atlassian’s data shows the gap between using AI and embedding it, and METR’s shows self-reports can mislead. Ask each team which recurring tasks now run on a tested prompt or skill, what their verification catch rate is and whether discovery volume has risen.

How to apply it

Here’s a five-week method for moving from ad hoc AI use to an embedded, verified way of working, for yourself first and then for your team.

Week 1: Map the work.

  1. List every recurring activity in your job for a typical month: discovery calls, ticket reviews, PRDs, metrics reviews, competitive tracking, stakeholder updates, meeting prep, business reviews, release notes, launch readiness. Note how often each happens and roughly how long it takes.
  2. For each activity, fill in the AI workflow map: the AI’s role (draft, synthesize, critique, monitor, prototype or none), its frontier position (inside, edge, outside), the context and sources it needs, the verification check, the human-only step and the current rung on the automation ladder.
  3. Mark three activities to change first. Pick at least one upstream activity (discovery synthesis, win/loss or ticket mining), one recurring report and one drafting task. Starting only with drafting repeats the production gap.

Week 2: Build the context pack.

  1. Collect your Product 360 artifacts. Write the always-loaded brief: product one-liner, personas, North Star and input metrics with current values and dates, strategy pillars and non-goals, this quarter’s outcomes, pricing summary, glossary, house style and decision rights. Keep it to one or two pages.
  2. List the referenced documents the harness should load on demand, with their location, owner and confidentiality class.
  3. Load the pack into a shared project in your approved harness. Test it with five questions you already know the answers to. Where the answers are wrong or generic, fix the brief, not the question.

Week 3: Connect and write the first entries.

  1. Request the connectors your three activities need, at the narrowest scope: read-only for CRM, tickets, call recordings, analytics and the backlog. Get write access only where an approval gate exists.
  2. Write a library entry for each of your three activities. Each has inputs, context, the prompt, an output format, what good looks like, pass or fail checks and two or three test inputs drawn from real past work.
  3. Run each prompt on the test inputs. Compare the output with what you produced by hand last time. Record the failures you see as “known failure modes” in the entry.

Week 4: Verify and climb.

  1. Use each prompt for real at least twice, running the checks every time. Track two numbers per entry: how often a check catches something, and how much editing the output needed.
  2. Promote any entry that’s stable to the next rung. A saved prompt becomes part of the shared project; a weekly report becomes a scheduled task that delivers a draft you review. Don’t promote anything whose checks still catch serious errors.
  3. Write your weekly operating routine: which AI-assisted tasks run on which day, and which human step follows each.

Week 5: Bring the team.

  1. Draft the team’s AI usage policy with product ops, security and legal: approved tools and connectors, data classes, verification standards, disclosure rules, agent rules and the do-not-delegate list.
  2. Move your library entries into a shared team library, ask every PM to contribute two, and name an owner. Promote any prompt that two or more PMs use weekly into a team skill.
  3. Hold a 30-minute monthly review: what AI got wrong, which checks caught it, which entries to retire, refine or promote, and whether the outcomes you care about moved. Then keep the routine going.

Prompts for every major PM task

The Prompts section below has ten fully specified prompts. This table covers the wider set of tasks a PM’s library should include. Each row is a starting request; build it into a full library entry before it becomes a routine.

PM task What to ask the harness Check
Interview guide Draft a guide that tests the problem, asks about past events and never pitches No “would you” questions; nothing about our solution
Interview synthesis Cluster themes across transcripts with call IDs, counts per persona and single-source flags Spot-check three quotes against the recordings
Said versus did Contrast what customers say they want with what usage data shows they do Each contrast cites both a quote and a metric
Support ticket mining Group tickets by job and pain, by segment, with volumes and examples Sample ten tickets per cluster; check the grouping
Win/loss Extract reasons won and lost by segment and competitor, separating stated from inferred reasons Inferred reasons are labeled; counts match the source list
Assumption mapping List assumptions under this bet and the cheapest test for each Top-right items are the ones that would kill the bet
Strategy red team Attack this strategy for value, usability, feasibility and viability risk; play our toughest competitor You can answer each attack or you change the plan
Product coaching Coach me on this decision using our strategy; point out my mistakes; don’t reassure me The critique names specific gaps, not generic advice
PRD and narrative Interview me until you can write the brief; then draft from the brief in a fresh session The draft adds no scope, dates or claims you didn’t give
Edge-case mapping List error, empty, permission, loading, limit and failure states for this flow Engineering confirms the list before build
Prototype spec Turn this brief into a clickable prototype spec, or three divergent concepts Each concept tests a different assumption
Metric movement Give ranked hypotheses for this change and the evidence that would disprove each No causal claim without a cited comparison
Chart audit Check whether this chart supports the claim written above it Definitions, time range and denominator stated
Competitive monitoring Diff competitor release notes, pricing and docs since last week, with dated sources Every claim has a date and source
Battlecard update Update this battlecard from the week’s diff and recent win/loss Removed claims are listed, not just added ones
Stakeholder pre-read Predict each stakeholder’s likely objections and the evidence they’ll want Objections are specific to the person’s goals
Meeting follow-up Turn these notes into decisions, owners, dates and open questions Nothing appears that wasn’t decided in the room
Exec update Draft this week’s update in our fixed format from the connected sources Every number traces to a source and date
Bad-news draft Draft a message explaining this slip, for me to rewrite You rewrite it in your own words before sending
Business review prep Outline the QBR pack from CRM, usage and support data for this account Account facts checked against the CRM by you
Launch readiness Compare the launch tracker against our readiness checklist and list gaps Each gap names an owner
Release notes Write release notes in house style from these merged tickets No unreleased items; customer-facing language only
Post-launch review Compare launch outcomes with the PRD’s success criteria Uses the PRD’s metrics, not new ones
On-rampIf you're new to working with a harness

Start with one habit for two weeks: before you write anything, ask the harness to interview you about it, then have it write the brief from your answers. You’ll keep the thinking yours and still get the speed. Then add one recurring report.

The AI lens

Building AI-powered products

This chapter has been about your own work, but if you build AI products, your own AI use is the cheapest lab you have.

  • You are a user of the patterns you ship. Every frustration you have with a harness (generic answers without context, confident errors, agents that act too freely, prompts that drift) is a frustration your customers will have with your product. Keep a log. It’s free discovery for Chapter 31’s trust and autonomy decisions.
  • The context pack is a product pattern. If your AI feature underperforms, ask whether it has the equivalent of your context pack: the customer’s own definitions, history and constraints, kept short, with the rest retrieved when needed. Many quality problems in AI features are context problems.
  • Your verification standard is an eval in miniature. Pass or fail checks on your own documents are the same discipline as the graders in your product’s eval suite. PMs who verify their own AI output tend to write better eval criteria, because they’ve felt the difference between “looks right” and “is right.”
  • Connectors and skills are distribution. If customers’ harnesses can reach your product through MCP, a well-designed connector or skill becomes a channel. Chapter 14 covers that platform question; your own connector use tells you what a good one feels like.

Doing the work with AI

Use the harness on the system itself, not just the tasks inside it.

  • Audit the library. Once a month, give the harness the library and the month’s failure log. Ask which entries are duplicates, which lack checks, which failure modes recur and which prompts should merge or retire.
  • Draft your own workflow map. Connect your calendar and documents and ask what recurring work you did last month, how long each took and which items fit the inside-the-frontier profile. Correct it; it won’t know what mattered.
  • Draft the context pack. Give it your Product 360 artifacts and ask for a two-page brief with every number dated and every gap marked. Then cut it yourself. Models tend to keep too much.
  • Red-team the usage policy. Ask the harness to play a careless PM and a malicious email, and list the ways each could leak data or trigger an unwanted action under the draft policy.
The AI lensThe one-line rule

Give AI the context, the task and a check to run. Keep the decision, the relationship and your name on the result.

The Beacon case: the AI-augmented Principal PM

Beacon caseWhere you start

You’re three months into the Principal PM role on Beacon. Your AI use is ad hoc: a chat for drafting emails, long conversations you can’t find again, and metrics screenshots pasted in on Monday mornings. Meanwhile, the Beacon Agents launch at Northlight Live is approaching, the pricing move to per-resolved-incident needs a narrative, and the wrong-rollback incident (Chapter 31) has made everyone, including you, more careful about trusting AI output.

The workflow map. You list fourteen recurring activities. Three stand out. Discovery synthesis is mostly undone: you have more customer calls recorded than you’ve watched. The Monday metrics review takes two hours of pulling numbers before any thinking starts. And competitive tracking happens only when a deal is lost. You pick those three, plus the pricing narrative as your drafting task.

The context pack. The brief fits on two pages. It holds the North Star (incidents resolved with Beacon’s help per week); the input metrics (diagnosis acceptance rate, autonomous resolution rate, MTTR, alert-to-incident compression and weekly active responders), each with a current value and date; the five personas (Priya, Dana, Marcus, Sam and Leo); ARR of about $48M growing 38%; NRR of 118%; gross margin of 72% since the agentic launch; the pricing move; and the open strategic tension between building on Northlight Observe data and staying tool-agnostic. Referenced files include the wrong-rollback review, the Beacon Classic sunset plan and the log of EU customers’ AI Act documentation requests. Before loading it, you mark the incident review “internal, no customer names” and keep the customer-identifying version out of the shared project.

Connectors. With Northlight’s security team, you request read-only connectors for call recordings, support tickets, CRM, product analytics and the backlog. Write access to the backlog waits for an approval step. The security reviewer asks the questions Sam asks of Beacon: what can it reach, what does it log, how do we revoke it.

Discovery synthesis. You run the synthesis prompt over 30 recent customer calls about the Beacon Agents approval gate. The harness clusters concerns by persona: security reviewers want audit logs and least-privilege credentials; on-call engineers want an answer they can act on in under five minutes; the MSP persona wants per-tenant views. Your check (every quote needs a call ID and must appear verbatim in that call) catches one problem: a vivid “quote” about kill switches that no transcript contains. The model had blended two customers’ remarks into one sentence. The team rule becomes “quotes need a call ID,” and it goes into the usage policy.

The near miss. Two weeks later, a scheduled task drafts a QBR pack for a key account. The summary says the account’s MTTR improved by a third since adopting Beacon Agents. Your verification check (every number traces to a named source) fails: the analytics source shows the improvement only for incidents where the diagnosis was accepted, a much smaller set. You correct the claim before the account’s VP of IT Operations sees it. The echo with the wrong rollback isn’t lost on you. Beacon’s agent proposed a confident root cause the evidence didn’t support; your own harness did the same with a number. You apply to your own work the eval discipline you demand of the product.

The pricing narrative. For the per-resolved-incident pricing brief, you ask the harness to interview you until it can write the brief. It asks twenty questions, three of which you can’t answer well (how credits work when the agent makes an incident worse, how MSPs bill their own customers, what happens to margin at high volumes). Those become your homework before you write anything. In a fresh session, the harness drafts the narrative from the brief; a third session reviews it against the brief and plays two critics, Marcus’s CFO and Leo worrying about MSP margin. You rewrite the opening and the recommendation yourself.

The routine and the team. By week five, a Monday scheduled task delivers a metrics digest against the context pack, with “what changed” and ranked hypotheses. You write the “so what” and the decisions. A Friday task delivers a competitive diff with dated sources. Beacon’s three PMs, the designer and the product ops lead build a shared library; the product ops lead becomes the Lab. Two prompts, release notes in house style and the weekly metrics narrative, become team skills after a month of stable use. The team policy forbids pasting customer incident data into unapproved tools and requires read-only connectors for anything production-adjacent, which makes Northlight’s own security review easy.

What stays human. When the customer affected by the wrong rollback asks for a briefing on what changed, the harness helps you build the timeline and check every date against the incident record. You run the conversation yourself, on a call, and you answer the hard questions without a script. Go or no-go for Beacon Agents at Northlight Live is also yours: the harness drafts the readiness pack from the launch tracker, and you make the call with the VP of Product.

## 4. Data classes
| Class | Examples | Where it may go |
|---|---|---|
