Product 360 health review and maturity score Review All 37, Appendix C 37-health-review

Three details differ from Chapter 00’s list. The stakeholder map moves to the front, because you need to know whom to grill. The decision log opens on day 1, though the full cadence (spine 10) waits for the third phase; the first scope dispute needs somewhere to go. And the roadmap follows the North Star and OKRs, because a roadmap you can’t trace to a measure of success is a list of features.

For product leadersFor product leaders: running this across a portfolio

If several PMs are building 360s at once, standardize the moves, not the content: the same master grilling prompt, challenge tests and health review template for everyone, packaged as a reusable skill or saved prompt. The portfolio review can then compare dimensions across products. Chapter 28 covers how product operations can own that kit.

Keeping it alive

The 90 days end with a running cadence. Chapter 00 defined the rhythm (weekly, biweekly, monthly, quarterly, annual and per event) and two rules: every ritual produces a decision or is cancelled, and decisions get written down. Chapter 29 covers governance and business reviews in depth.

The harness lowers what maintenance costs, and the weekly review shows how. In Cedric Chin’s account of Amazon’s weekly business review, informed by former Amazon executive Colin Bryar, the same graphs appear every week so people learn what normal variation looks like; owners say “nothing to see here” for routine lines, explain the exceptions, or admit they don’t know yet and schedule the follow-up. Chapter 18 builds that pack. This chapter’s maintenance prompt has the harness draft the weekly brief from connected sources as exceptions only: what moved outside its normal range and the likely reason, or “unknown, owner investigating.” You verify the numbers and add the judgment.

The other rhythms follow Chapter 00’s artifact kinds. Living artifacts (roadmap, metrics, OKRs, competitive landscape, stakeholder map) get a quarterly re-grill: a short session on what changed. Durable artifacts (vision, strategy, personas, positioning, lifecycle stage) get an annual re-grill, or an early one when an event forces it. Each re-grill starts from the last log and asks only what’s changed.

Scoring maturity

Appendix C gives a maturity model for scoring your 360 dimension by dimension and finding the weakest one. Its shape borrows from the Capability Maturity Model that Watts Humphrey and the Software Engineering Institute at Carnegie Mellon developed from 1986, with five levels from ad hoc to continuously improving. Only the shape is borrowed; the Product 360 levels are this book’s own.

You can ask the questions behind the scale of any dimension before you open Appendix C. Does an artifact exist? Does it have an owner and a review date? Is it current, with cited sources? Does a ritual make decisions from it? Is it consistent with the other artifacts and readable by the harness? Each “yes” is a step up. The day-90 health review asks these across all nine dimensions, scores them against Appendix C and picks the weakest as next quarter’s focus.

How to apply it: the 90-day plan

The plan assumes you’ve taken over an existing product. For a new product the order holds, but the intake is thinner and more of the gap list is decisions.

Before day 1: set up the workspace.

  1. Create a Product 360 workspace in your harness: a project, folder or repository with standing instructions and a place for the artifacts. The instructions hold the scope paragraph (draft it now, even if it’s wrong), the nine dimensions, the seven challenge tests and the no-invention rule. Use the workspace prompt and the workspace brief template; Chapter 32 covers how harnesses carry instructions across sessions.
  2. Confirm which connectors and tools are approved for customer and financial data, and connect only those.

Days 1 to 30: learn and anchor.

  1. Scope the surface area (Chapter 00, step 1). Send the scope paragraph to your manager and the PMs on your boundaries. Log any dispute as decision log entry 1. You now have a decision log.
  2. Run the intake. Point the harness at your documents, ticketing, CRM, analytics and finance sources, or supply exports where connectors don’t exist, each labeled with name, owner and date. Run the intake prompt, then review the gap list and correct anything misfiled before it drives the grilling. This is the first human gate.
  3. Draft the Product 360 index (spine 1) with Chapter 00’s index prompt. Mark everything you haven’t verified as “unverified” and publish it to your team in week 2, half-empty and honest.
  4. Build the stakeholder map and a first DACI (spine 12, Chapters 28 and 36). The harness can draft it from org charts, meeting invites and decision history; you correct it from conversations. It tells you whom to send file-mode questions to.
  5. Run a listening tour alongside the intake: your manager, peers on the boundaries, engineering and design leads, sales, customer success, product marketing, finance and at least five customers across the buying group (Chapter 01). Ask each what’s working, what’s broken and what decision is overdue. Add the notes to the workspace, with permission and an approved tool.
  6. Grill the facts only. Run short sessions that confirm or correct the “facts found” list, and send file-mode questionnaires to the owners of “facts missing.” Hold off on strategy; you don’t yet know enough to argue with your own answers.
  7. Land one early decision. Pick the overdue decision with the clearest owner and the most evidence (often a scope boundary or an unowned metric), write a decision memo (Chapter 17), get it decided and log it. That’s Watkins’s early win, in the form a B2B product allows.
  8. Agree on expectations with your manager at day 30: the gap list, the order for the next 60 days and what you will deliberately not do in the first 90.

Days 31 to 60: decide and build the spine.

  1. Grill dimension by dimension, in dependency order: Customer, Strategy, Business, Measure, Build, Go-to-market, and AI for an AI-powered product. Use the master grilling prompt with the module for each dimension, live for judgment-heavy dimensions and file mode for anything a stakeholder must answer. Approve each log before you use it; this is the second human gate.
  2. Generate the artifacts in a fresh session, one at a time, with the artifact generation prompt and the template named in the build order table. Every claim carries a source tag; anything unsourced stays as a visible gap. Record each artifact’s owner and review date in the build tracker.
  3. Share drafts with the people who’ll live with them (the business model with finance, the AI risk assessment with security and legal, and so on). Treat their objections as new grilling input and log them.
  4. Run the day-60 consistency audit. Each contradiction becomes a fix (the artifact was wrong) or a decision log entry (the conflict is real and someone must choose). This is the third human gate.

Days 61 to 90: operate and prove.

  1. Formalize the cadence (spine 10). Put the weekly metrics review, monthly roadmap refresh and quarterly business review on the calendar, each with the artifacts it reviews and the decision it produces (Chapters 00 and 29). Start the weekly exception brief with the maintenance prompt and run at least four cycles before day 90.
  2. Assess the lifecycle stage (spine 11, Chapter 30) of each offering in scope, legacy ones included. That’s where inherited products hide their liabilities.
  3. Produce the event artifacts the calendar demands: PRDs and PR/FAQs (Chapters 04 and 34), launch plans (Chapter 25), event plans (Chapter 26), sunset plans (Chapter 30), AI PRD addenda (Chapter 31). Generate them from the spine. When an event artifact contradicts the spine, take the conflict to the decision log.
  4. Hold the business review on the 360. Present from the index and spine artifacts rather than a deck built for the occasion (Chapter 35). A slide the 360 can’t support marks a gap.
  5. Run the Product 360 health review: each dimension’s freshness, open grilling items and maturity score against Appendix C. Pick the weakest dimension as next quarter’s focus.
  6. Run a premortem on the next quarter, write the next 90-day plan and close this one.
Key ideaThree human gates

The harness does most of the mechanical work, but three approvals stay with you: the gap list before grilling, each session log before generation, and the audit before publishing. Skip one and the harness’s mistakes reach artifacts other people treat as true.

The AI lens

When the product is AI-powered

An AI-powered product needs a tenth grilling module. Chapter 00 explains why AI isn’t a tenth dimension; the module exists because AI reaches into four of the nine at once, and each needs an artifact from Chapter 31.

  • Measure: the eval plan. What does “good” mean for this AI feature, who decided, what are the current scores and what score stops a release? A PM who can’t answer doesn’t yet know whether the product works.
  • Business: the AI cost model. What does one task or one resolved outcome cost in inference, and which way is it trending? AI features can quietly change unit economics, as Beacon’s gross margin shows.
  • Lifecycle: the model and vendor register. Which models and versions are in use, with which deprecation dates? A model retirement is a lifecycle event your customers will feel even if you change nothing.
  • Operate: the AI risk assessment. What are the failure modes, guardrails and regulatory duties (Chapter 33)? The question that matters most: what’s the worst thing this product has already done, and what changed afterward?

The premortem works especially well here. “It’s 90 days from now and the agent caused an incident at a customer. What happened?” produces eval cases, guardrails and risk entries in one pass, and often exposes the gap between what the positioning promises and what the risk assessment allows.

Doing the work with AI

Most of this chapter is about doing the work with AI. Five rules keep it honest.

The harness asks; you decide. If the harness starts answering its own questions with confident judgments, stop and restate the rule. If you catch yourself accepting every recommendation without reading the reasoning, slow down: an untouched recommendation is still your decision, logged under your name.

Split sessions and write things down. Each grilling session covers one dimension and ends in a written log. Generation happens in a fresh session that reads the approved log and the cited sources: the interview, write, then build pattern Anthropic recommends for coding work.

Make the audit a separate pass. Shehzaad Dhuliawala and colleagues at Meta AI showed in 2023 that a model hallucinates less when it drafts an answer, plans questions to verify its own claims, answers them independently so the draft doesn’t bias them, and then revises. They called it Chain-of-Verification. The consistency audit prompt follows that shape, and Chapter 19’s verification checklist covers the numbers in more depth.

Package what you repeat. You’ll run the master grilling prompt and the maintenance prompt dozens of times. Save them where your harness keeps reusable instructions: a skill, a saved prompt or a project’s standing instructions. Anthropic’s Agent Skills, introduced in October 2025, and similar features elsewhere load packaged instructions only when relevant (Chapter 32). Packaging also lets a portfolio leader give every PM the same session.

Keep the 360 machine-readable. After day 90, the maintenance prompts read the index and only the artifacts due for review. That works only if the index is current and the artifacts are documents the harness can open (Chapter 00).

The AI lensWhat the harness shouldn't touch

The harness drafts the gap list, the questions, the artifacts and the briefs. It doesn’t approve any of them, it doesn’t appear as the decider in the decision log, and it doesn’t send anything to a stakeholder on your behalf without you reading it first.

The Beacon case: the first 90 days

Beacon casePicking up where Chapter 00 left off

Chapter 00 covered your first two weeks as Principal PM for Beacon: the scope paragraph, the 140-document inventory, the Northlight Observe boundary dispute logged as decision 1, and a first QBR showing an index with twelve linked artifacts (four new, five repaired, three “stale, owner assigned”) and six decision log entries. Linked isn’t the same as decided. This is how the twelve became true by the next business review, near day 90.

Days 1 to 30: intake and the first grilling. You connect the harness to the documentation wiki, the roadmap in the ticketing system, the CRM, the analytics platform and an FP&A model export, all on tools approved for Northlight’s confidential data, and run the intake. The facts-missing column includes the current autonomous resolution rate by segment and inference cost per resolved incident, which nobody owns yet (Chapter 18 later gives it owners in finance and product). The decisions-missing column has four items: the North Star definition, the pricing metric, the Observe boundary and the end-of-life date for Beacon Classic.

The first live session is Business, because gross margin is the most visible problem. The harness opens with a fact, cited from the FP&A export: gross margin fell from 81% to 72% after the agentic features launched, because of inference cost. Its first decision question: what gross margin must Beacon Agents reach for a per-resolved-incident price to be viable? The recommendation comes with reasoning from the export and a note that the strategy deck still assumes 80%.

You answer “back to 80%.” The harness challenges on two tests. Evidenced: 81% was the pre-agent level; what inference cost per incident does 80% imply, and is there evidence it’s reachable? Owned: who is accountable for the cost side? You don’t know the cost figure and say so. The item is logged as open, owner the applied AI lead, with your note: “80% is a target to test, not a commitment.” The premortem produces the line that shapes the next two months: the new price launches at Northlight Live and margin falls further.

Meanwhile you draft the stakeholder map: Priya, Dana, Marcus, Sam and Leo outside; your manager (the VP of Product for the Operations portfolio), the Observe and Desk group PMs, the product marketing manager, product ops and finance inside. The first DACI covers the Observe boundary, with your manager as approver.

That boundary becomes your early win. The listening tour shows that both teams want a clean story for customers who run both products; the disagreement is about who owns the correlation roadmap. Your memo proposes, and your manager approves, that Beacon keeps its Correlate team and owns diagnosis and action, while correlation of Observe-native alerts becomes a shared capability with a joint quarterly roadmap review. Decision 1 closes in week 4, consistent with the guiding policy you’ll write in Chapter 03: Observe data as an accelerant, not a requirement.

Days 31 to 60: grilling the spine. The Customer session runs alongside the discovery work in Chapter 01. When you answer “SRE teams” to the question of who the customer is, the harness challenges on Specific: SRE teams use Beacon, but who signs, who blocks and who resells? Marcus, Sam and Leo enter the persona set, and Sam’s job story comes from Chapter 01’s interviews.

The Measure session starts from the North Star: incidents resolved with Beacon’s help per week. The harness accepts the metric and challenges the phrase “with Beacon’s help.” An accepted diagnosis, an approved action or both? If per-resolved-incident pricing goes ahead, this definition becomes the price meter. You log it as open with a two-week deadline; the definition you later agree with finance and product marketing is the one in Chapter 18. The session also names diagnosis acceptance rate and autonomous resolution rate as inputs to the metric tree (Chapter 02).

The AI session anchors its premortem in a real event: the design-partner pilot in which a responder accepted a hallucinated root cause and rolled back the wrong service (Chapter 31). The eval plan, the guardrails and the AI risk assessment all take cases from it. Sam’s requirements become audit-log and least-privilege items in the risk assessment, and the EU customers’ requests for AI Act documentation go into its regulatory section (Chapter 33).

You generate the artifacts one at a time in fresh sessions. The day-60 consistency audit then finds two contradictions that no single artifact would have revealed. First, the positioning draft promises “autonomous remediation,” while the AI risk assessment allows autonomy only for low-risk actions on a customer’s allowlist. Second, the roadmap still carries a feature investment in Beacon Classic, while the draft lifecycle assessment puts Classic in decline. Both become decision log entries. The positioning changes to “supervised remediation” (Chapter 24). The Classic feature is cut, and its team moves to migration tooling (Chapter 30).

Days 61 to 90: running it. The cadence goes on the calendar. The weekly exception brief covers the North Star, MTTR, diagnosis acceptance rate, autonomous resolution rate, weekly active responders and inference cost per resolved incident. The maintenance prompt drafts it from the connected sources each Monday, and you check every number before it’s shared. In one of the first four cycles, the brief flags diagnosis acceptance sliding while weekly active responders rise; Chapter 19 tells how the team traced it to the mix of accounts migrated from Classic rather than to agent quality. The brief surfaced the exception and named an owner the same week.

The event artifacts arrive on time because the spine already holds their inputs: the Beacon Agents launch and event plans for Northlight Live (Chapters 25 and 26) draw on positioning, personas and the risk assessment, and the Classic sunset plan (Chapter 30) on the lifecycle assessment.

At day 90 you run the health review. Measure and Business come out strongest: both have owners, are current and feed a ritual that decides from them. Leadership has a map and a DACI but no ritual that uses them yet. Lifecycle is weakest: Classic has an assessment and a sunset plan, but nobody has assessed Correlate and Diagnose as offerings in their own right. Scored against Appendix C, Lifecycle sits at the bottom, so it becomes next quarter’s focus, with a re-grill in week 2.

The 360 still isn’t complete. Three artifacts are marked “current, owner assigned, re-grill due.” But every artifact traces to a log entry or a source, every contradiction the audit found is fixed or in the decision log, and anyone who asks what Beacon’s North Star is gets the same answer from you, from the index and from the harness.

Product 360 artifacts

Five artifacts carry the 90 days. The 30/60/90 plan sets the commitments, the build tracker shows progress, the grilling session log holds the decisions, the health review scores the result, and the workspace brief gives the harness its standing instructions. The spine artifacts themselves use the templates from the chapters named in the build order table.

# Product 360 workspace brief · [Product]

Standing instructions for the AI harness. Keep this short and current; it loads with every session.

## Scope
[The scope paragraph, with the date it was last confirmed.]

## Where the 360 lives
- Index: [location]
- Grilling logs: [location]
- Decision log: [location]
- Approved connectors: [list, with what each may be used for]
- Not approved for this workspace: [systems or data types]

## Rules
1. Never invent facts, numbers, quotes or decisions. If a source doesn't support it, say "no source" and add it to the gap list.
2. Fetch facts from connected sources and cite them (source, owner, date). Ask the PM only for decisions.
3. Ask one question at a time, with a recommended answer and the reason.
4. Test every answer against the seven challenge tests: specific, evidenced, falsifiable, trade-off named, consistent, owned, decision-relevant. Push once on a failure, then log it as open or overridden.
5. Don't agree to be agreeable. If the evidence points elsewhere, say so.
6. Write every session to a grilling log before ending it.
7. The decision log names a person as the decider, never the harness.

## Vocabulary
- Nine dimensions: Customer, Strategy, Business, Build, Measure, Go-to-market, Operate, Lifecycle, Leadership.
- Artifact kinds: durable, living, event.

Prompts

These eight prompts form a chain: set up the workspace, run the intake, grill with the master prompt plus a dimension module, generate the artifacts, audit them, maintain them and review their health. They work in any capable harness. Every one of them can touch customer data, unreleased financials or confidential strategy, so run them only in a harness and with connectors your company has approved for that data. Chapter 00’s prompts (inventory, index, cadence and contradiction check) and Chapter 32’s context-pack prompt complement this set.

✦ PromptSet up the Product 360 workspace
Goal: Give the harness standing instructions so every later session follows the same rules.
Paste in: your scope paragraph, the list of approved connectors and data types, where the index and logs will live, and any existing metric dictionary. Use only a harness approved for your company's confidential data.

You're helping me build and maintain a Product 360 for [product surface area]. Draft a workspace brief that will load with every session in this workspace. Use the structure below and keep it under 600 words.

1. Scope: restate my scope paragraph. List any boundary that looks disputed or vague, as a question for me.
2. Where things live: the index, grilling logs, decision log and approved connectors, with what each connector may be used for. List anything I've said is not approved.
3. Rules for you, in this order:
   - Never invent facts, numbers, quotes or decisions. If no source supports something, say "no source" and add it to the gap list.
   - Fetch facts from connected sources and cite source, owner and date. Ask me only for decisions, priorities and trade-offs.
   - Ask one question at a time, each with your recommended answer and the reason.
   - Test every answer I give against seven tests: specific, evidenced, falsifiable, trade-off named, consistent, owned, decision-relevant. On a failure, name the test and push once. On a second failure, log the item as open or overridden with my reason.
   - Don't agree with me to be agreeable. If the evidence points elsewhere, say so plainly.
   - Write every session to a grilling log before it ends.
   - The decision log always names a person as decider, never you.
4. Vocabulary: the nine dimensions (Customer, Strategy, Business, Build, Measure, Go-to-market, Operate, Lifecycle, Leadership) and three artifact kinds (durable, living, event).
5. Current state: phase, open items, next review due.

Then ask me up to three questions about anything in the brief you couldn't fill from what I gave you.

[scope paragraph, connectors, locations, metric dictionary]

Check the output: read the rules section aloud. If any rule lets the harness answer a decision question on its own, or accept an answer without testing it, rewrite that rule before saving the brief.
✦ PromptRun the intake and produce a gap list
Goal: Turn the documents and data you inherited into an evidence map and the agenda for every grilling session.
Paste in (or connect): strategy decks, PRDs, pricing pages, QBR and board decks, roadmap exports, dashboard exports, finance model exports, win/loss and support escalation summaries, your listening tour notes. Label each item with its name, owner and date. Put the documents first and this prompt after them. Use only approved tools; remove personal identifiers from customer material.

[documents, each labeled: name | owner | date]

You're running the intake for the Product 360 of [product]. Work in four passes and show each one.

Pass 1, evidence. For each of the nine dimensions, quote the passages from the documents that state a fact about the product (numbers, dates, owners, definitions, commitments, decisions already made). Give each quote its source name and date. Don't summarize yet.

Pass 2, conflicts and staleness. List every place where two sources disagree, or where a source is older than a later event it doesn't reflect. For each, give both quotes and dates.

Pass 3, the gap list. Produce one table per dimension with three sections:
- Facts found: the fact, the quote, the source, the date, and "confirm with [owner]".
- Facts missing: what's missing, the likely owner and the system that probably holds it.
- Decisions missing: phrased as a question I must answer, with why it matters in the next quarter.

Pass 4, the agenda. Propose the order of grilling sessions, starting with the dimension carrying the most business risk, and say why. Mark which sessions should be live and which should go to a stakeholder as a written questionnaire, and to whom.

Rules: every fact in Pass 3 must trace to a Pass 1 quote. If you're inferring rather than quoting, label it "inference." Never fill a gap with a plausible guess.

Check the output: pick five facts at random and open their sources. If any quote is wrong or any "fact" came from inference, rerun Pass 3 with a stricter instruction. Then move anything misfiled between facts and decisions before you approve the list.
✦ PromptMaster grilling session
Goal: Draw out the decisions behind one dimension of your Product 360, one question at a time, with the harness challenging weak answers and writing everything down.
Paste in: the workspace brief, the approved gap list for this dimension, earlier grilling logs that this dimension depends on, the dimension module from the next prompt, and any reference materials not already connected. Use only approved tools.

You're going to grill me about the [dimension] dimension of the Product 360 for [product]. The goal is a grilling log complete enough that a fresh session could generate the [artifact names] from it without asking me anything else. Stop when every question in the module and every decision-missing item in the gap list is agreed, overridden or open with an owner, or when I say stop.

How to run the session:
1. Before asking anything, list the facts you'll rely on from the gap list and connected sources, with citations, and ask me to confirm or correct them in one reply.
2. Then walk the decisions in dependency order: settle the questions other answers depend on first. Ask exactly one question per turn.
3. With each question, give your recommended answer and the reasoning, citing evidence where it exists. If the evidence is thin, say so and recommend anyway.
4. Never ask me for a fact a connected source can answer. Look it up, cite it and ask me to confirm.
5. Test each of my answers against the seven tests: specific, evidenced, falsifiable, trade-off named, consistent (with my earlier answers and existing artifacts), owned, decision-relevant. If an answer fails, name the test and explain the gap in two sentences, then ask again. If my second answer still fails, log it as "overridden" with my reason, or "open" with an owner, and move on. Don't argue a third time.
6. Don't agree with me to be agreeable. If I contradict the evidence or an earlier answer, say so before moving on.
7. If I say "I don't know," ask who would know, log it as "needs owner" and continue.
8. Every five questions, show a two-line running summary so I can correct drift.
9. When the questions are done, run a premortem: "It's 90 days from now and this dimension's artifact misled a decision. What happened?" Ask me for my answer, then add the two failure stories you think are most likely, and ask what we should change.
10. Finish with a readback of everything decided, ask me to confirm it, and then write the grilling log with these columns: Q-ID, question, kind (fact or decision), your recommendation and reason, my answer, evidence, challenge raised, status (agreed, overridden, open, needs owner), owner, feeds artifact. Add the overrides table, the premortem and the readback.

File mode: if I say "file mode," don't ask live. Instead write every question for this dimension into a questionnaire, each with your recommended answer, the reason and a blank "Your answer" line, addressed to [stakeholder]. When I paste back the edited file, treat untouched recommendations as accepted, test every edited answer against the seven tests, ask follow-ups only for failures (one at a time), and then write the log.

Start with step 1.

Check the output: before you approve the log, scan the status column. If every item is "agreed," the harness probably went easy on you; rerun the challenge step on your three most important answers. Make sure no "agreed" answer is a fact that nobody actually confirmed.

✦ PromptGenerate a Product 360 artifact from grilling logs
Goal: Turn approved grilling answers and evidence into one of the book's templates, without adding anything that wasn't decided or sourced.
Paste in: in a fresh session, the workspace brief, the approved grilling log(s) for this artifact, the cited source documents and the empty template from this book (for example, the strategy one-pager from Chapter 03). Use only approved tools.

[grilling logs]
[source documents, each labeled: name | owner | date]
[template]

Fill in the [template name] for [product] using only the grilling logs and sources above.

Rules:
1. Every sentence or table cell that states a fact, number or decision ends with a source tag: the log Q-ID (for example [STR-07]) or the document name and date.
2. Use "overridden" answers as written, and add the override note in a comment so readers know a challenge was raised.
3. Where the template asks for something the logs and sources don't cover, write "GAP: [what's missing] (owner: [name or unknown])." Don't fill it.
4. Don't add facts, examples, competitors, numbers or quotes that aren't in the material.
5. Keep the template's headings and order. Write in plain language, short sentences.

After the artifact, list: (a) every GAP, (b) every place where two log answers seemed to conflict and how you handled it, (c) any open item from the log that this artifact depends on.

Check the output: pick five source tags and confirm each one supports the sentence it's attached to. Search for any sentence without a tag. Either it's connective text or it was invented; delete the second kind.
✦ PromptAudit the Product 360 for consistency
Goal: Find contradictions, unsourced numbers and stale content across the whole 360 before anyone else does.
Paste in: the Product 360 index and every spine and AI artifact (or connect the harness to where they live), plus the decision log. Use only approved tools.

Audit the Product 360 for [product]. Work in separate passes and don't let an earlier pass change a later one's answers.

Pass 1, claims. List every factual claim and number in the artifacts, with the artifact and section it appears in.

Pass 2, verification questions. For each claim, write the question that would verify it ("What is the gross margin in the latest finance export?"). Then answer each question independently from the cited source alone, without looking at the artifact's wording. Mark each claim verified, unsourced, contradicted by its source, or stale (the source is older than a later event).

Pass 3, cross-artifact contradictions. Check these pairs at minimum: positioning against the AI risk assessment and current capability; roadmap against strategy one-pager and lifecycle assessment; OKRs against the North Star tree; business model against pricing and the AI cost model; personas against positioning and the stakeholder map; the decision log against every artifact a decision touched. Quote both sides of each contradiction.

Pass 4, coverage. Which spine artifacts are missing, have no owner, or are past their review date?

Output a table: issue, artifacts affected, quotes, type (unsourced, contradicted, stale, missing, cross-artifact), severity (blocks a decision this quarter / should fix / cosmetic), and a proposed resolution: "fix the artifact" if the source is clear, or "decision needed: [question], decider: [name]" if the conflict is real.

Check the output: every "decision needed" row goes into the decision log with a decider and a date. Spot-check three "verified" claims yourself; if any fails, rerun Pass 2 for that artifact.
✦ PromptMaintain the Product 360 on its cadence
Goal: Keep the 360 true with the least effort: an exception-only weekly brief, a monthly roadmap check and scheduled re-grills.
Paste in: the workspace brief and the Product 360 index; the harness loads only the artifacts due for the chosen mode. Name the mode. Use only approved tools.

Mode: [weekly / monthly / quarterly / annual / event]

Weekly: From the connected metric sources, draft an exception brief for [product]'s weekly review. Use the same metrics in the same order every week: [list from the North Star tree]. For each, say "nothing to see here" if it moved within its normal range over the last eight weeks, or, if it didn't, give the size of the move, the likely reason with evidence, or "unknown, owner [name] investigating." Add new risks, decisions logged this week and any artifact whose review date passed. Keep it to one page.

Monthly: Compare the roadmap against the strategy one-pager, the OKRs and last month's decisions. List items that no longer trace to an outcome, items that changed without a decision log entry, and competitive or customer changes from the month that should affect the roadmap.

Quarterly: Load the living artifacts (roadmap, metric tree, OKRs, competitive landscape, business model, stakeholder map) and their last grilling logs. Run a short grilling session: for each artifact, ask what changed since the last log, with your recommended update and evidence, one question at a time, using the seven tests. Write a new log that references the previous one.

Annual: Do the same for the durable artifacts (vision and strategy, personas, positioning, lifecycle stage), and add one question per artifact: "If we were writing this from scratch today, would we write the same thing?"

Event: For [launch / sunset / pricing change / reorganization / incident], list every spine artifact the event affects and the questions each now needs answered, then start a grilling session on the first one.

Rules: verify every number against its source and show the source. Don't restate unchanged content. Don't propose decisions; frame them as questions with a recommended answer.

Check the output: check every number in the weekly brief against the dashboard before you share it. If the brief runs past one page, it's a recap, not an exception brief; cut it back.
✦ PromptDraft the Product 360 health review
Goal: Score the 360 dimension by dimension against Appendix C and pick next quarter's focus.
Paste in: the Product 360 index, the build tracker, the latest consistency audit, the grilling logs' open items, the decision log and calendar evidence of which rituals were held, and the Appendix C maturity model. Use only approved tools.

Draft a Product 360 health review for [product] for [quarter], using the health review template.

For each of the nine dimensions (and the AI artifacts if applicable):
1. List the artifacts, owners and last-reviewed dates from the tracker.
2. Mark freshness: current, stale or contradicted, citing the audit.
3. Name the ritual that made a decision from this dimension's artifacts this quarter, citing the decision log. If none, say "not used."
4. Score maturity against Appendix C, quoting the level description you matched and the evidence for it. If evidence is mixed, give the lower level and say why.
5. Count open grilling items and open audit contradictions.

Then: cadence health (rituals held against planned, decisions produced, which to keep, change or cancel); AI artifact health (eval trend, cost trend, deprecations due); the weakest dimension with your reasoning; and three fixes, each with a suggested owner and date.

Finally, ask me three grilling questions, one at a time with recommended answers, to confirm the weakest dimension and the fixes before you finalize the review.

Check the output: challenge any score above the level the evidence supports; generous scores defeat the purpose. Make sure the weakest dimension is chosen by evidence, not by which one is most comfortable to fix.

Anti-patterns

Anti-patternThe marathon session

One conversation tries to grill all nine dimensions in an afternoon. By the third hour the harness has lost early answers and the PM is accepting recommendations to get it over with. Grill one dimension per session and write the log before you stop.

Anti-patternThe agreeable harness

Every answer is marked “agreed,” every recommendation was accepted, and the artifacts read beautifully. Nothing was tested. Give the harness explicit challenge tests, tell it not to agree for its own sake, and treat a log with no challenges as a log to rerun.

Anti-patternAsking the PM for facts

The harness asks you for ARR, launch dates and ticket counts, and you answer from memory. Some of those answers are wrong, and they’re now in durable artifacts with your name on them. Facts come from connected sources, with citations; you confirm them. You answer decisions.

Anti-patternGenerating before deciding

Skipping the grilling and asking the harness to “write our strategy from these docs.” The result blends real facts, invented ones and decisions nobody made, and it’s fluent enough that nobody notices. Grill first; generate from the approved log.

Anti-patternTemplate theater at speed

With a harness you can fill every spine and AI template in a day, and get a complete-looking 360 that nobody has decided, owned or reviewed. Now that drafting costs almost nothing, Chapter 00’s warning matters more: an artifact counts only when its decisions are logged and its owner has a review date.

Anti-patternFeature wins in the first 90 days

A new Principal PM tries to prove themselves by shipping something in the first quarter. In an enterprise release cycle, what ships was mostly decided before they arrived. Aim the early win at a decision unblocked and recorded.

Anti-patternThe 360 that stops at day 90

The build was a project with a finish line, and the cadence never started. Three months later the artifacts are as stale as the ones you inherited. The 90 days end with rituals on the calendar and re-grills scheduled, not with a published folder.

Checklist

Key takeaways

  • A Principal PM’s first 90 days produce decisions more than features. Build the Product 360 to make those decisions visible, owned and durable: learn and anchor, then decide and build the spine, then operate and prove.
  • Separate facts from decisions. The harness fetches and cites facts through connectors; you supply decisions; anything neither sourced nor decided stays visible as a gap.
  • The grilling session is the core technique: one question at a time, a recommended answer from the evidence, challenges against seven explicit tests and a written log. Run it per dimension, live for judgment and in file mode for stakeholders.
  • Anchor the harness in labeled reference materials before you grill, and generate artifacts in a fresh session from the approved log. Keep three human gates: the gap list, the log and the audit.
  • Audit the artifacts against each other as well as against their sources. The most useful findings are contradictions between positioning and risk, or between roadmap and lifecycle, and each one becomes a fix or a logged decision.
  • Day 90 ends with a running cadence, a health review scored against Appendix C and the weakest dimension chosen as next quarter’s focus.
C
Appendices

Product 360 Maturity Model

Score your product's 360 and find the weakest dimension.

26 min read · 2 templates · 3 prompts

A Product 360 is never finished, so "is it done?" is the wrong question. The useful questions are how mature each dimension is and which one is holding the product back. This appendix gives you a five-level scale, a table for each of the nine dimensions that says what each level looks like in documents you can open, an overlay for AI-powered products, and the templates and prompts to score your 360 every quarter.

NoteThis is the book's own model

The maturity levels, criteria and scoring rules in this appendix are The Product 360 Handbook’s framework, not an industry standard. As Chapter 37 notes, the five-level shape borrows from the Capability Maturity Model that Watts Humphrey and the Software Engineering Institute developed; the content of each level is this book’s.

How to use the model

Score each of the nine dimensions separately, from evidence. A score is the highest level whose criteria the dimension meets in full, along with every level below it. If you can’t show a document, a calendar entry or a decision log line for a criterion, it doesn’t count. When evidence is mixed, take the lower level and write down why.

Then find the two weakest dimensions. Don’t average the nine scores. A product with Measure at 5 and Lifecycle at 1 averages 3, and the average hides a well-instrumented dashboard sitting next to an end-of-life notice that will surprise customers. The weakest dimension is where the next unpleasant question will come from, so it’s where your next quarter of 360 work goes.

When two dimensions tie for weakest, break the tie with the gap list from Chapter 00: pick the one with the higher business risk or the nearer fixed date (a launch, a renewal wave, a regulatory deadline).

For each of the two weakest dimensions, plan to move up one level in the next quarter. Each dimension table below names the chapters that teach the move. One level is the right ambition: jumping from 1 to 4 means building an artifact and a ritual and a decision habit at once, and the ritual usually dies first.

Re-score every quarter, as part of the quarterly business review or the Product 360 health review in Chapter 37. Keep the previous scores next to the new ones. A dimension that slips a level is telling you something specific: an owner left, a ritual stopped, or an event (a pricing change, a reorg, a model deprecation) made a durable artifact false.

Four rules keep the scores honest:

  • Evidence over intent. “We review the roadmap monthly” counts only if the calendar shows the last three reviews happened and the decision log shows what they decided.
  • Score the whole scope. If personas cover the direct business but not the partner channel, the dimension is only partly defined. Score the weakest part that’s in scope.
  • Level 5 takes time. A dimension reaches level 5 only after holding level 4 for at least two consecutive quarters.
  • Someone else checks. Ask a peer PM, your manager or product ops to challenge your scores, or run the challenge prompt later in this appendix. It’s easy to score your own work generously.
On-rampIf you're new to product management

You don’t need every dimension at level 5. Level 3 or 4 across the board, with one or two dimensions lower for a known reason, is a healthy 360. The model is for deciding where to spend your next hour of 360 work, not for grading yourself.

The five levels

The levels follow the questions Chapter 37 asks of any dimension. Does an artifact exist? Does it have an owner and a review date? Is it current, with cited sources? Does a ritual make decisions from it? Is it consistent with the other artifacts and readable by a harness, and does it get better each cycle? Each “yes” is a step up.

Level Name What it means The test
1 Absent No artifact answers the dimension’s question. The answer lives in someone’s head, a meeting or a slide from a past planning cycle. Ask three people the dimension’s question and you get three answers.
2 Ad hoc An artifact exists but was written for one event, covers only part of the scope, has no named owner or review date, or is stale or contradicted by another artifact. You can open a document, but you can’t say who keeps it true or when it last was.
3 Defined The spine artifacts for the dimension exist, cover the whole scope, name an owner and a review date, are current and cite their sources. Anyone can open the artifact from the Product 360 index and trust it today.
4 Managed A named ritual reviews the artifacts on their cadence, decisions made from them are in the decision log, and stale items are flagged and fixed within one cycle. The calendar and the decision log show the artifact being used to decide something.
5 Compounding The artifacts have held level 4 for two or more quarters, pass a consistency audit against neighboring dimensions, are readable by an approved AI harness, and each cycle’s outcomes feed back into them. The artifact is measurably better than a year ago, and the next decision it supports takes less effort than the last.

The step from 3 to 4 is the easiest to miss. A defined artifact that no ritual uses decays quietly, because nobody notices it going stale until an executive asks a question it should answer. The step from 4 to 5 is about learning: post-launch reviews update the personas, experiment readouts update the metric tree, and missed forecasts update the business model.

The nine dimensions

Each table describes what you can observe at each level, the artifacts that indicate it and the chapters that teach the move to the next level. Template ids in code font refer to Appendix A.

1. Customer

Who is this for, and what job are they hiring it to do?

Level What you can observe Artifacts that indicate it Read to move up
1 Absent Sales, engineering and product describe the customer differently. No written problem statement exists. None, or a persona slide nobody can source Ch. 01
2 Ad hoc Personas exist but cover users only, or date from a past launch. Discovery happens before big releases and stops after. Interview notes sit in personal folders. Persona deck without owner or date; scattered interview notes Ch. 01, 10
3 Defined A problem hypothesis and personas cover users, the economic buyer and gatekeepers such as security reviewers. Each persona cites interviews or data from the last year and names an owner. product-hypothesis, b2b-persona, job-statements, journey-map Ch. 01, 17, 27
4 Managed Discovery runs on a standing cadence. The weekly team sync reviews the discovery log, and roadmap and positioning decisions in the log cite customer evidence. interview-snapshot, discovery log, 10-insight-brief, decision log entries citing evidence Ch. 09, 21, 27
5 Compounding Post-launch reviews, support themes and win/loss findings change the personas and the hypothesis, and the change history shows it. Killed hypotheses are recorded with the evidence that killed them. 09-voc-report, 13-win-loss-analysis, 27-feature-request-triage-policy, persona change history Hold the level; re-grill yearly (Ch. 37)

2. Strategy

Where do we play, how do we win, and what will we say no to?

Level What you can observe Artifacts that indicate it Read to move up
1 Absent The strategy is whatever the last executive review approved. The team can’t name what it has decided not to do. None, or a vision line on an all-hands slide Ch. 02, 03
2 Ad hoc A strategy deck exists from the last planning cycle but no longer matches the roadmap or the market. Competitor knowledge is anecdotal. Last year’s strategy deck; ad hoc competitor notes Ch. 02, 03, 13
3 Defined A one-page strategy states the diagnosis, the guiding policy and the explicit no’s. A competitive landscape covers the real alternatives, including doing nothing. Both have an owner and a review date. 02-vision-statement, 03-strategy-kernel, 03-strategy-one-pager, 13-competitive-landscape Ch. 03, 16, 29
4 Managed The monthly product review checks roadmap changes against the one-pager. The competitive landscape is refreshed quarterly, and strategic changes go through the decision log rather than drifting in. Decision log entries that cite the strategy; 16-competitive-threat-monitor; quarterly landscape updates Ch. 14, 16, 20
5 Compounding Each annual refresh records which strategic bets paid off and which didn’t, and the next strategy reflects it. Moat and platform assessments are revisited with evidence. 16-seven-powers-assessment, 16-moat-scorecard, 14-platform-map, 29-annual-plan-narrative Hold the level; annual re-grill (Ch. 37)

3. Business

How does this make money, and is the money worth it?

Level What you can observe Artifacts that indicate it Read to move up
1 Absent The PM can’t state revenue, margin or the pricing metric without asking finance. None Ch. 13, 15
2 Ad hoc A business case exists from the original funding decision, or finance owns a model the PM has never opened. Pricing exists but nobody has written down why. Original business case; a finance model; a price list Ch. 12, 13, 15
3 Defined A business model and unit economics summary shows revenue, growth, gross margin, the pricing metric and the main cost drivers, reconciled with finance’s numbers and owned by the PM. 13-business-case, 15-value-metric-assessment, 12-evc-model Ch. 15, 29
4 Managed The quarterly business review walks the summary. Pricing and packaging changes go through a written proposal and the decision log. Variances between plan and actual get an owner. 29-qbr-outline, 15-pricing-packaging-proposal, 15-price-change-impact-plan, decision log Ch. 09, 12, 15
5 Compounding Forecasts are compared with actuals each quarter and the model’s assumptions are updated. Pricing changes are measured after launch, and the results shape the next change. 09-clv-model-brief, 12-lifecycle-pricing-plan, price-change readouts Hold the level; annual re-grill (Ch. 37)

4. Build

What are we building next, and how does it get made?

Level What you can observe Artifacts that indicate it Read to move up
1 Absent The plan is the ticket backlog. Nobody can say what ships next quarter or why. Ticket queue only Ch. 03, 06
2 Ad hoc A roadmap exists as a feature list with dates, often several versions for different audiences. PRDs are written for some features and not updated when the scope changes. Feature-and-date roadmap; PRDs that describe what was planned, not what shipped Ch. 03, 04, 06
3 Defined An outcome roadmap (now, next, later) traces each item to a strategic choice and a metric. PRDs and PR/FAQs follow a standard template, and a backlog policy says how items get in and out. 03-now-next-later-roadmap, 04-prd, 34-pr-faq, 03-backlog-policy, 06-release-plan Ch. 06, 11, 28
4 Managed The monthly roadmap refresh and biweekly sprint reviews change the plan from evidence, and cuts are logged. Technical debt is a visible line in planning, not a surprise. 11-cycle-review, 06-tech-debt-register, 03-roadmap-communication-pack, decision log Ch. 05, 07, 11
5 Compounding Post-launch reviews compare each release with the outcome its PRD promised, and the gap informs how the next bets are sized. The team’s delivery process is itself reviewed and adjusted. 05-post-launch-review, 05-iteration-plan, 11-process-health-check Hold the level; quarterly re-grill (Ch. 37)

5. Measure

How do we know it’s working?

Level What you can observe Artifacts that indicate it Read to move up
1 Absent No agreed definition of success. Different teams quote different numbers for the same thing. None, or vendor default dashboards Ch. 02, 05
2 Ad hoc Dashboards exist with dozens of charts but no North Star. Metrics are pulled for a review and then ignored. Definitions live in the analyst’s head. Large dashboard; one-off analyses Ch. 02, 05, 17
3 Defined A North Star and input metric tree are written down with definitions, owners and sources. OKRs tie to the tree. Event tracking follows a tracking plan. 02-north-star-tree, 02-okr-set, 05-tracking-plan, 18-metric-dictionary Ch. 18, 19, 29
4 Managed A weekly metrics review walks the same pack every week, explains exceptions and assigns owners. Experiments have pre-registered designs and written readouts. Numbers in executive reviews are checked against source. 18-weekly-business-review-pack, 29-weekly-business-review, 05-experiment-design, 05-ab-readout, 19-verification-checklist Ch. 05, 09, 17
5 Compounding Metric definitions are revised when they stop predicting outcomes, and the change is logged. Experiment results update the metric tree. The harness can answer routine metric questions from connected, trusted sources. 17-decision-review, 18-data-trust-check, metric tree change history Hold the level; quarterly re-grill (Ch. 37)

6. Go-to-market

How does it reach, convince and keep customers?

Level What you can observe Artifacts that indicate it Read to move up
1 Absent Sales describes the product in its own words, differently by region. Launches happen when engineering finishes. None Ch. 24, 25
2 Ad hoc Positioning exists from an earlier version of the product. Launch materials are built per launch with no tiering. Enablement is a slide deck and a recorded call. Old positioning doc; one-off launch decks Ch. 24, 25, 27
3 Defined Positioning and messaging reflect the current product and its real competitive alternatives. Launches are tiered, with a plan and readiness criteria. Claims are substantiated. 24-positioning-statement, 24-messaging-framework, 24-claims-log, 25-launch-plan, 27-sales-enablement-kit Ch. 25, 26, 27
4 Managed Launch go/no-go meetings decide from readiness evidence. Field feedback and win/loss reach the product team on a cadence and change the roadmap or the messaging. Go/no-go records, 27-feature-request-triage-policy, 13-win-loss-analysis, 27-customer-onboarding-plan Ch. 08, 26, 27
5 Compounding Each launch and event has an impact report that changes how the next one is planned. Positioning is tested against win/loss evidence and revised at the annual refresh. 26-event-impact-report, 05-post-launch-review, 08-attribution-assessment Hold the level; annual re-grill (Ch. 37)

7. Operate

How do we run it week to week?

Level What you can observe Artifacts that indicate it Read to move up
1 Absent Meetings exist but have no fixed agenda or output. Decisions are made in chat and forgotten. Recurring meetings only Ch. 28, 29
2 Ad hoc Some rituals have agendas. A decision log or risk register was started and abandoned. Escalations go to whoever is loudest. Abandoned decision log or risk register Ch. 28, 29
3 Defined An operating cadence names each ritual, its attendees, the artifacts it reviews and the decision it produces. The decision log and risk register exist and are current. operating-cadence, 29-decision-log, 29-risk-register, 29-escalation-policy Ch. 28, 29
4 Managed The rituals happen as planned, and each produces logged decisions. The risk register is reviewed in a ritual, and rituals that stop producing decisions get cut. Calendar history, 29-monthly-product-review, 28-daci-decision, decision log with recent entries Ch. 28, 32
5 Compounding The cadence is reviewed each quarter and changed from evidence (attendance, decisions produced). Routine briefs are drafted by an approved harness and checked by people, which frees the rituals for judgment. 11-process-health-check, 32-weekly-ai-routine, 28-tool-stack-map Hold the level; quarterly review (Ch. 37)

8. Lifecycle

Where is it in its life, and what happens next?

Level What you can observe Artifacts that indicate it Read to move up
1 Absent Nobody has stated the product’s lifecycle stage. Legacy versions and old features have no end-of-life plan, and customers are the ones asking. None Ch. 30
2 Ad hoc A stage assessment or sunset plan exists for one offering, usually the one causing escalations, but not for the rest of the scope. One sunset plan or end-of-sale notice Ch. 30
3 Defined Every offering in scope has a lifecycle stage assessment with evidence. Stage-gate criteria say what triggers a move to the next stage. 30-lifecycle-stage-assessment, 30-stage-gate-criteria, 30-end-of-life-plan Ch. 29, 30
4 Managed The quarterly business review or portfolio review checks each offering’s stage and gate criteria. Sunset decisions are logged with a migration plan and customer communication. 29-portfolio-review, 30-sunset-decision-memo, 30-migration-plan, 30-deprecation-communication-plan Ch. 10, 12, 23
5 Compounding Lessons from each sunset or relaunch change the gate criteria. Pricing, investment and staffing follow the stage, and the record shows it. 12-lifecycle-pricing-plan, 10-relaunch-plan, 23-scale-up-readiness-checklist Hold the level; annual re-grill (Ch. 37)

9. Leadership

Who needs to be aligned, and are they?

Level What you can observe Artifacts that indicate it Read to move up
1 Absent The PM learns who can block a decision when they block it. Ownership boundaries with neighboring teams are unclear. None Ch. 36
2 Ad hoc A stakeholder list exists, often an org chart excerpt. Decision rights are argued case by case. Contact list; email threads Ch. 28, 36
3 Defined A stakeholder map shows influence and position. Major decisions have a DACI with one approver. Boundaries with neighboring products are written and agreed. 36-stakeholder-map, 36-daci-decision, 36-team-charter Ch. 34, 35, 36
4 Managed The stakeholder map is reviewed quarterly and drives an engagement plan. Executive communications follow a plan and a standard format, and their outcomes are logged. 36-stakeholder-engagement-plan, 35-executive-briefing-outline, 34-decision-memo, decision log Ch. 34, 35, 36
5 Compounding Alignment problems are caught before decisions, not after. The team charter and coaching plans are updated from what each quarter taught. Stakeholders use the 360 index to answer their own questions. 36-pm-competency-self-assessment, 36-one-on-one-coaching, index access history Hold the level; quarterly re-grill (Ch. 37)
For product leadersFor product leaders: comparing products

In a portfolio, ask every PM to score with this appendix and bring the evidence, not just the numbers. Compare dimensions across products rather than totals. When several products share a weak dimension, the cause is often in the portfolio’s own operating model, and the fix belongs to you or to product operations (Chapter 28), not to each PM separately.

The AI overlay

For an AI-powered product, Chapter 00 adds four artifacts to the spine, and each lives in a dimension: the eval plan in Measure, the AI cost model in Business, the model and vendor register in Lifecycle and the AI risk assessment in Operate. Score each of the four on its own with the table below, and record it next to its host dimension.

When an AI element scores lower than its host dimension, keep both scores and treat the gap as a candidate for one of the two weakest. A Measure dimension at level 4 with an eval plan at level 2 means the dashboard is trusted while nobody can say whether the AI’s answers are any good. A customer can find that gap before you do.

Level Evals (Measure) Cost (Business) Model register (Lifecycle) AI risk (Operate)
1 Absent Quality is judged by demos and anecdotes. No eval set exists. Nobody knows what one task or outcome costs in inference. Nobody can list which models and versions are in production. No written failure modes. Guardrails exist only in code.
2 Ad hoc An eval set exists for one feature or was built once before launch and not rerun. “Good” isn’t defined in writing. Inference cost appears as a line in the cloud bill, not per task, user or outcome. A list of models exists but lacks versions, owners or deprecation dates. A risk review was done for launch and not revisited. Regulatory duties are unknown or assumed.
3 Defined An eval plan defines “good” for each AI feature, names who decided it, and records current scores and the score that blocks a release. Cases come from real failures. An AI cost model shows cost per task or outcome, its trend and its effect on gross margin, reconciled with finance. The register lists every model and version, the vendor, the owner and known deprecation dates. An AI risk assessment lists failure modes, guardrails, human approval points and regulatory duties by market, with an owner.
4 Managed Evals run before every release and gate it. A monthly AI quality and cost review tracks scores against production signals. Cost per outcome is in the weekly or monthly review, with an owner for variance. Pricing decisions cite it. Deprecation dates feed the roadmap and the lifecycle review, and a runbook covers model changes. A ritual reviews the risk assessment, incidents update it, and launch go/no-go uses it.
5 Compounding Production failures and post-incident reviews add eval cases every cycle. Eval scores predict customer-visible quality. Cost forecasts are compared with actuals, and model or architecture choices are made from the trend. Model swaps have been run through the runbook at least once, and lessons changed it. Red-team findings and incidents feed back into guardrails and the eval set. Regulatory documentation is produced from the assessment, not written fresh each time.

Chapters to read to move up: Chapter 31 for all four artifacts; Chapter 28 for the monthly AI quality and cost review (28-ai-quality-cost-review); Chapter 15 for pricing that covers inference cost (15-ai-pricing-model-comparison); Chapter 30 for the model deprecation runbook (30-model-deprecation-runbook); and Chapter 33 for impact assessments, red-teaming and incident response (33-ai-impact-assessment, 33-red-team-plan, 33-ai-incident-response-plan).

The AI lensScoring with a harness

A harness connected to your 360 can do most of the evidence gathering: find each artifact, read its owner and review date, check the calendar for rituals and match decision log entries to artifacts. It can’t tell whether a ritual’s decisions were good, and it can count a passing mention as an artifact unless you tell it not to. Use the prompts below to draft the scores, then check the evidence for every score of 4 or 5 yourself. Use only tools approved for the data your 360 contains.

The Beacon case: scoring at day 90

Beacon caseBeacon's first maturity score

Chapter 37 ends Beacon’s first 90 days with a health review. This is that review’s maturity scoring, using the tables above. All Beacon facts are fictional and come from the running case.

At day 90 you score Beacon’s 360 with the scoring prompt, then check every score yourself against the evidence it cites. Two scores come down a level when you open the cited documents: the harness had counted the scheduled monthly product review as held, and it had read the Beacon Classic sunset plan as covering every offering.

Dimension Level Evidence What blocks the next level
Customer 3 Defined Personas now include Marcus (economic buyer), Sam (security reviewer) and Leo (MSP partner) alongside Priya and Dana. Sam’s job story comes from the Chapter 01 interviews. No roadmap or positioning decision in the log cites the discovery log yet.
Strategy 3 Defined The strategy one-pager states the guiding policy (Observe data as an accelerant, not a requirement), and the competitive landscape is current. The roadmap was checked against the one-pager by the day-60 audit, not by a ritual.
Business 4 Managed The business model summary is reconciled with the FP&A export (gross margin down from 81% to 72%). Inference cost per resolved incident is in the weekly brief. The 80% margin target is logged as open with an owner. Level 5 needs two quarters at level 4 and a forecast-to-actual comparison.
Build 3 Defined The outcome roadmap follows the North Star and OKRs. The Beacon Classic feature cut is logged. The monthly roadmap refresh hasn’t yet completed a cycle that changed the plan from evidence.
Measure 4 Managed The North Star definition is agreed with finance and product marketing. The weekly exception brief has run four cycles and flagged the drop in diagnosis acceptance rate, with an owner, the same week. Level 5 needs two quarters at level 4 and a logged revision history for metric definitions.
Go-to-market 3 Defined Positioning now says “supervised remediation.” Launch and event plans for Northlight Live exist. The launch go/no-go hasn’t happened, and field feedback doesn’t yet reach the product team on a cadence.
Operate 3 Defined The cadence is on the calendar, the decision log is active and the weekly brief runs. The risk register and the AI risk assessment aren’t reviewed in any ritual; the weekly brief covers metrics only.
Lifecycle 2 Ad hoc Beacon Classic has a stage assessment and a sunset plan. Correlate and Diagnose have no stage assessment as offerings in their own right.
Leadership 3 Defined The stakeholder map and the DACI for the Observe boundary exist. The boundary is agreed, with a joint quarterly roadmap review. No ritual uses the stakeholder map yet.

The AI overlay adds four scores: cost at level 4 (it’s in the weekly brief, and the pricing work cites it), and evals, the model register and AI risk at level 3. Each exists with an owner, and the eval plan and risk assessment take cases from the hallucinated root cause in the design-partner pilot. None of the three is reviewed in a ritual yet. Evals at 3 under a Measure score of 4 is exactly the gap the overlay is meant to show.

The two weakest. Lifecycle, at 2, is the clear first choice. Six dimensions tie at 3, so the tie-break decides the second. Beacon Agents goes live at Northlight Live with supervised remediation in customers’ production environments, and no ritual reviews the AI risk assessment. Go-to-market shares that fixed date, but an agent acting in production without a reviewed risk assessment carries the higher business risk, so Operate is the second focus.

The plan for next quarter, one level each:

  • Lifecycle, 2 to 3. Assess Correlate and Diagnose with the lifecycle stage assessment, write stage-gate criteria for all three offerings and re-grill the dimension in week 2 (Chapters 30 and 37).
  • Operate, 3 to 4. Add the risk register and the AI risk assessment to the monthly product review, and make the AI risk assessment an input to the Northlight Live go/no-go (Chapters 29 and 33).
  • Watch item, not a focus. Add eval scores to the monthly review so the eval plan can reach level 4 alongside Measure (Chapter 31).

Nothing else gets new 360 work this quarter. The other dimensions keep their cadence and get re-scored at the next review.

Prompts

✦ PromptScore a Product 360 from its documents
Goal: Draft a maturity score for each dimension from evidence, ready for you to check.
Paste in (or connect the harness to): the Product 360 index, the artifacts it links, the decision log, the operating cadence and calendar evidence of which rituals were held, last quarter's self-assessment if one exists, and the level tables from Appendix C. This material is usually confidential; use only tools approved for it.

You are helping a product manager score the Product 360 for [product] against the maturity model in Appendix C of The Product 360 Handbook. The model has five levels: 1 Absent, 2 Ad hoc, 3 Defined, 4 Managed, 5 Compounding. The nine dimensions are Customer, Strategy, Business, Build, Measure, Go-to-market, Operate, Lifecycle and Leadership.

For each dimension:
1. List the evidence you found: artifact name, owner, last-reviewed date, the ritual that reviews it (if any) and decision log entries that cite it. Give a source for each item.
2. Test the level criteria from level 2 upward, and stop at the first level whose criteria are not all met. Quote the criterion that failed.
3. Give the score. If evidence is mixed, give the lower level and say why. Give level 5 only if earlier assessments show level 4 held for two consecutive quarters.
4. Rate your confidence (high, medium, low) and name any evidence you could not open or date.

Rules:
- A passing mention of a topic in another document is not an artifact.
- A meeting on the calendar is not a held ritual unless notes or decision log entries show it happened.
- Score the weakest part of the scope.

If the product is AI-powered, score the four AI elements (evals, cost, model register, AI risk) against the AI overlay the same way, and flag any that score below their host dimension.

Finish with a table of all scores, the two weakest dimensions (break ties by business risk or nearest fixed date, and say which you used) and a list of evidence gaps for me to check.

[Appendix C level tables]
[Product 360 index and artifacts]
[decision log, cadence, calendar evidence]

Check the output: open the evidence cited for every score of 4 or 5 and confirm the ritual actually ran and decided something. Confirm that no level 3 rests on an artifact without an owner or review date. If the harness's scores and yours differ, record the reason in the self-assessment.
✦ PromptTurn maturity scores into a quarterly improvement plan
Goal: Get a realistic one-quarter plan that moves the two weakest dimensions up one level each.
Paste in: the completed self-assessment, the Appendix C tables for the two weakest dimensions, the operating cadence, the next quarter's fixed dates (launches, reviews, renewals, regulatory deadlines) and the team's available time.

My Product 360 for [product] scored [scores]. The two weakest dimensions are [dimension 1, level] and [dimension 2, level].

For each of the two:
1. List the criteria from the next level up that are not yet met, quoting the Appendix C table.
2. Propose no more than four actions that would meet those criteria. For each, give the artifact or template to build or repair, the ritual that will use it, an owner role, a due date inside the quarter and the evidence that will show it's done.
3. Flag any action that needs a decision or time from someone outside the product team, and name who.

Then:
- List anything you'd deliberately not do this quarter, and why.
- Estimate the hours per week the plan costs the PM.

Do not propose moving any dimension more than one level, and do not add actions for dimensions other than these two unless one of them blocks the plan.

Check the output: every action should trace to an unmet criterion. If the PM hours look higher than you can spend, cut actions rather than stretching dates past the quarter.
✦ PromptChallenge a self-assessed maturity score
Goal: Find the scores you've inflated before your manager or a peer does.
Paste in: your completed self-assessment with its evidence links, and the Appendix C level tables. Use only approved tools.

Act as a skeptical reviewer of this Product 360 self-assessment for [product]. For each dimension scored 3 or higher:
1. Argue that the score should be one level lower. Use the Appendix C criteria and the evidence provided, and name the weakest piece of evidence.
2. Ask me one question that would settle it.

Don't change any score yourself. Don't invent evidence for or against. If the evidence for a score is strong, say so in one line and move on.

[self-assessment]
[Appendix C level tables]

Check the output: answer each question with evidence, not explanation. Lower any score you can't defend, and record each challenge and its resolution in the self-assessment.

Appendices

Glossary

The vocabulary of product management, defined plainly.

60 min read

This glossary defines the terms the book uses, in the sense the book uses them. Each entry gives a short definition and points to the chapter or chapters where the term does real work, so you can go from a word you half remember to the method behind it. Named frameworks keep their originators' names, as the chapters do. Where a term has a broader meaning in the industry, the definition here is the narrower one that the chapters apply to B2B, enterprise and platform products. Abbreviations appear in parentheses after the term. Most are filed under the full name; a few that the book always uses in short form, such as RICE and DACI, are filed under the abbreviation.

A

AARRR (pirate metrics): Dave McClure’s five stages of a customer’s life with a product: acquisition, activation, retention, referral and revenue. In B2B each stage needs a reading for accounts and buying groups rather than individual visitors. See Chapters 05 and 08.

Acceptance criteria: The details that show whether a story was completed correctly, in Mike Cohn’s definition; they can be examples, rules, tests or brief notes. Writing them in Given, When, Then form forces each requirement into something a test or an eval can check. See Chapters 06 and 10.

Acqui-hire: Buying a company mainly for its team, used when you need a team or capability faster than you can build it. License-and-hire is the variant that licenses the technology and hires the people without buying the company. See Chapter 22.

Actionable metrics: Metrics that show clear cause and effect, usually by cohort, so a team can tell what to do next. Eric Ries set them against vanity metrics. See Chapters 17 and 21.

Activation: The moment a new user or account first gets real value, defined as a specific completed action that delivers that value. In enterprise products it is never a login, and for AI products it usually means an accepted output. See Chapters 05 and 08.

Adoptability: The fourth risk that B2B products carry beyond desirability, feasibility and viability: whether the buying group, the security review and procurement will let the product through. See Chapter 01.

Agent: An AI system in which the model directs its own process and tool use, in a loop, based on what it observes. Erik Schluntz and Barry Zhang of Anthropic distinguish agents from workflows, which follow predefined code paths. See Chapters 31 and 32.

Agent2Agent protocol (A2A): A protocol created by Google and announced in April 2025 for agents to talk to other agents across organizations. It became a Linux Foundation project in June 2025 and complements MCP, which connects agents to tools. See Chapters 14 and 31.

Agile Manifesto: The statement of values and principles for software development written in February 2001 by seventeen practitioners, among them Kent Beck, Martin Fowler, Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland. See Chapter 11.

AI cost model: The artifact that tracks what one task, user or resolved outcome costs in inference, and which way that cost is trending. It belongs to the Business dimension of the Product 360. See Chapters 00 and 31.

AI literacy: A duty under the EU AI Act, applying from February 2025, to make sure the people who build and use AI systems understand them well enough. Minimal-risk systems carry no specific duties beyond it. See Chapter 33.

AI PRD: A PRD for an AI-powered feature. It keeps every section of a classic PRD and adds evals with pass-rate targets as acceptance criteria, a failure taxonomy, latency budgets, cost per task, trust and failure UX, staged autonomy with a kill switch, a gross-margin floor and regulatory classification. Chapter 04 calls the added sections the AI feature addendum. See Chapters 04 and 31.

AI risk assessment: The artifact that records an AI product’s failure modes, guardrails and regulatory obligations. It belongs to the Operate dimension of the Product 360. See Chapters 00 and 33.

Ambidextrous organization: Charles O’Reilly and Michael Tushman’s model in which separate exploratory units are integrated at the senior team, so new businesses get protection while the core shares its assets. See Chapters 20 and 23.

Anchoring: The bias by which an initial number pulls later estimates toward it, even when the number is arbitrary. The book rates it robust and applies it to the first price or first ROI figure a buyer sees. See Chapters 10 and 12.

Answer engine: An AI assistant that buyers use to research and shortlist vendors before they touch your website. The book’s answer engine audit runs a fixed set of buyer questions across the major assistants each month. See Chapter 08.

Appetite: Ryan Singer’s term in Shape Up for how much time the business is willing to spend on a problem. An estimate starts from a design and produces a number; an appetite starts from a number and shapes the design to fit. See Chapters 06 and 11.

Aspirational OKR: An OKR that describes how you would like the world to look. In the playbook the book follows, the expected average score is 0.7, variance is high and the OKR may carry across cycles. Committed OKRs, by contrast, are ones the team agrees will be achieved, with an expected score of 1.0; a miss calls for a blameless postmortem. See Chapter 02.

Assumption map: A two-by-two that plots a team’s assumptions by importance and by the evidence behind them. Assumptions in the top-right quadrant (important, little evidence) get tested first. See Chapters 01 and 21.

Atomic network: Andrew Chen’s term for the smallest network that is stable and can grow on its own. In B2B it is often one team, one account or one integration pair. See Chapter 14.

Automation ladder: This book’s six-rung path for moving PM work onto AI, from single prompts toward agents. You climb a rung only when the work on the rung below is stable; it is a Product 360 synthesis, not a published framework. See Chapter 32.

Autonomy levels: Kevin Feng, David McDonald and Amy Zhang’s five levels of AI agent autonomy, defined by the user’s role rather than the agent’s capability, starting from the user as operator who directs and decides. The book treats autonomy as a dial set per action, not per product. See Chapter 31.

B

Backlog: The store of candidate work for a product. This book splits it into three stores rather than one list: an inbox for raw requests, an opportunity backlog of customer problems and a delivery backlog of committed work. See Chapters 03 and 06.

Battlecard: A one-page, sales-facing summary of one competitive situation: why you win, the competitor’s pitch in its own words, landmine questions and proof. See Chapters 13 and 27.

Beachhead: In Geoffrey Moore’s method, one segment narrow enough to dominate. You deliver the whole product that segment needs, win references there and then expand into adjacent segments, like a row of bowling pins. See Chapters 13 and 24.

Beta: A pre-release stage before general availability. GitLab’s sequence of stages runs experiment, beta, limited availability and generally available; beta and preview terms usually carry no SLA. See Chapter 25.

Big Idea: A single sentence that states your point of view and what is at stake for the audience, written before you build a presentation. Nancy Duarte and Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic both use the term. See Chapter 35.

Bottom line up front (BLUF): The military writing convention of putting the conclusion, recommendation or request in the first lines, then the background. See Chapters 34 and 35.

Break-even volume test: A check run before any price change: how much volume can you lose, or must you gain, for the change to leave contribution flat? See Chapter 15.

Build, measure, learn: Eric Ries’s loop in Lean Startup: turn ideas into products, measure how customers respond and learn whether to pivot or persevere. The aim is to speed up the loop. See Chapters 05 and 21.

Build, partner or buy: The decision about how to acquire a capability. The book frames it as a sequence of questions, starting with whether internal resources are relevant and, if not, whether the resource can be borrowed by contract. See Chapter 22.
